☆ A block coordinate descent method for nonconvex multiobjective optimization under Hölder continuity
Lizet Santa Cruz Calderón, John Frank Matos Ascona, Vitaliano de Sousa Amaral, Danilo Rodrigues de Souza
In this paper, we propose a block coordinate descent method for unconstrained multiobjective optimization problems with possibly nonconvex objectives and Hölder continuous gradients, intended for large-scale instances, in which updating all the variables simultaneously is expensive. In each iteration, only one block is updated along a descent direction common to all objectives, obtained by minimizing the maximum of their regularized quadratic models. We show that, unlike the single-objective case, stationarity on each block does not imply Pareto stationarity, and that no method that updates only the blocks of a partition of the variables and is monotone in all the objectives reaches, in general, an $ε$-Pareto stationary point. Therefore, when none of the blockwise stationarity measures exceeds the tolerance, the algorithm performs a joint step across all coordinates and terminates only at $ε$-Pareto stationary points. We establish a complexity bound of $O(ε^{-(β+1)/β})$ iterations, where $β$ is the smallest Hölder exponent, the same order as that of methods that update all the variables, as well as bounds on the numbers of function and gradient evaluations, which also hold with one regularization parameter per block.
comment: 32 pages
☆ The Traveling Salesman Problem with non-convex polygonal neighborhoods: A hybrid Iterated Local Search--Block Coordinate Descent approach
Ernesto G. Birgin, Paula C. R. Ertel
The Traveling Salesman Problem with Neighborhoods (TSPN) generalizes the classical TSP by requiring a tour to visit a set of regions in the Euclidean plane rather than fixed point coordinates. It has applications in last-mile delivery, surveillance, and remote sensing in precision agriculture. In this paper, we address the Euclidean TSPN with arbitrary, non-convex polygonal neighborhoods---a highly complex setting due to the joint continuous and combinatorial optimization challenges. To solve the continuous subproblem of determining optimal visit points for a given visiting sequence, we propose a Block Coordinate Descent (BCD) method based on solving fast one-dimensional geometric subproblems. Computational experiments demonstrate that BCD computes optimal visit points for a fixed sequence in almost all instances in which optimality is certified, more than six orders of magnitude faster than a commercial solver solving the equivalent Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Programming (MIQCP) formulation. This efficiency enables an effective hybrid Iterated Local Search metaheuristic (ILS-BCD) that thoroughly explores the combinatorial search space at low computational cost. Extensive computational tests on 235 benchmark instances derived from the Generalized TSP (GTSP), with up to 100 neighborhoods, show that ILS-BCD matched or improved upon the best-known GTSP tours in all cases, obtaining strictly shorter tours in 234 instances. On the 80 instances for which optimality is proven, ILS-BCD attains the optimal tour length in all of them, within a relative difference below 0.001%. On 60 larger instances, with as many as 6,325 neighborhoods, ILS-BCD remains competitive up to about 220.
comment: 40 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Supplementary material available as an ancillary file
♻ ☆ Repair-Based Duality for Distributionally Robust Optimization via Conditional-Moment Optimal Transport
Louis L. Chen, Jake Roth
Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) models often admit dual representations that replace optimization over probability distributions with more tractable formulations, but estab- lishing primal-dual equality can be challenging when ambiguity sets involve conditional moment restrictions, noncompact uncertainty spaces, or unbounded losses. We study these questions through the conditional-moment optimal transport (CM-OT) framework, which encompasses transport-, divergence-, and jointly perturbed DRO models. Our main contribution is a repair- based sufficient condition for primal-dual equality. The approach constructs feasible couplings from nearly feasible ones by mixing with suitable reference couplings, while a local conditional uniform integrability condition on positive-loss tails ensures that the resulting repairs do not incur a nonvanishing loss in objective value. This establishes the closedness of the associated perturbation value function without relying on compactness or conventional interiority condi- tions. We further distinguish primal-dual equality from the additional steps required to obtain pointwise dual representations, providing conditions under which essentially bounded measurable conditional-moment multipliers can be replaced, at the level of optimal values, by bounded continuous multipliers and under which optimization and integration can be interchanged. Finally, we apply the framework to a class of DRO models combining divergence-based ambiguity with distributional calibration, including contextual resource-allocation and reliability applications.
comment: 34 pages
♻ ☆ Forgetting matters: when subspace optimization accelerates without the strong convexity parameter
Ilya Kuruzov, Ivan Dorofeev, Alexander Gasnikov
Sequential subspace optimization (SESOP) needs no problem constants, is accelerated on smooth convex functions and often accelerates in practice. One of our main contributions is to disprove the conjecture that it is uniformly accelerated on strongly convex functions. We develop a taxonomy of memory mechanisms by window length and forgetting rate. We consider exact subspace methods whose memory is a window of recent gradients and steps plus finitely many fixed cumulative sums. For this class, uniform acceleration requires either a window of length at least of order the square root of the condition number or a sum that forgets at a rate at least of order the inverse square root. For one fixed-factor filter pair with a bounded window this forgetting scale is necessary and sufficient up to constants. SESOP remembers too much and the plane form of conjugate gradients too little: neither is uniformly accelerated, even on infinitely differentiable functions quadratic near the minimizer. A short window converges locally quadratically over blocks when the Hessian is Lipschitz near the minimizer and equals a multiple of the identity plus a low-rank term there. Constructive upper bounds reach this forgetting scale without problem constants. Geometric filter pairs created at fixed times give uniform acceleration with logarithmic memory, also with inexact subproblems. A single pair with a smoothly adapted factor uses two vectors and attains an accelerated linear rate up to a prefactor polynomial in the condition number.
♻ ☆ Controlling discrete semilinear wave equations toward flocks
Sarah Strikwerda, Hung Vinh Tran, Minh-Binh Tran
We construct pointwise bounded controls that steer a finite, periodic, fully actuated active harmonic lattice with Rayleigh-Helmholtz velocity forcing to flock states in finite time. In our setting, an initial Lyapunov-feedback phase brings the velocities and elastic forces into a prescribed small neighborhood of zero. Then, subsequent trajectory planning and cancellation of the known drift achieve exact arrival at a moving flock. For prescribed stationary or moving profiles satisfying a strict control-admissibility condition, a two-stage interpolation reaches the target. We provide explicit sufficient time intervals for the stages following the initial feedback phase. Finally, we formulate the associated minimum-time problem and its formal Hamilton-Jacobi equation, leaving the continuity of the value function open.
♻ ☆ Deterministic Oracle Complexity for Goldstein Stationarity in Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization with Constraints
Yixi Ding, Ya-xiang Yuan
We consider the deterministic oracle complexity of finding a $(δ,ε)$-Goldstein stationary point of a Lipschitz function under constraints. Our main result concerns products of convex bodies. Each block contains an inner ball and lies in a concentric outer ball. The inner radii have a common positive lower bound, and each outer radius is at most a fixed multiple of the corresponding inner radius. This class includes common constraints such as balls and boxes. On each prescribed feasible set of dimension $d$ in this class, every deterministic algorithm using a local oracle needs $\exp(Ω(d))$ objective-oracle calls in the worst case at fixed, sufficiently small accuracies $δ$ and $ε$. The objective Lipschitz and initial objective-value gap bounds are fixed, and each constructed function has a global minimizer in the interior of the feasible set. For broader classes of constraints, supplementary results show that every deterministic algorithm needs $Ω(ε^{-2})$ objective-oracle calls in the worst case when $d\gtrsimε^{-2}$ and $δ\lesssimε$. The constants depend on the interior-ball radius and, for inequalities, the local Lipschitz and Slater bounds. These supplementary results cover closed sets that are star-shaped with respect to a ball and convex coercive inequalities with a Slater point, and hold even for convex objectives.
comment: 33 pages, no figures. Reformatted for journal submission; author information, funding, declarations and reference formatting updated. Mathematical results unchanged
♻ ★ Diffusion-Score-Based Joint Topology Identification and Generative Particle Filtering
Chuansen Peng, Hanning Tang, Xiaowei Yang, Xiaojing Shen
Inferring the interaction graph of a networked system while tracking its latent state is central to infrastructure, environmental, and brain networks. Joint identification of topology and latent states is challenging when observations are intermittent and transition noise is unknown and non-Gaussian: a flexible generative transition can absorb graph-induced changes of the conditional mean, whereas a Gaussian transition discards the information in the residual shape. We develop a diffusion-score-based framework for joint topology identification and generative particle filtering. The graph governs a leaky-diffusion conditional mean, and a frozen diffusion emulator represents the conditionally centered residual. First, a score--topology duality expresses edge-wise likelihood gradients as edge projections of the residual diffusion score, so topology learning requires neither transition densities nor differentiation through the sampler. Second, we prove identifiability from intermittent observations, invariance of the population minimizer across noise levels, and global strong convexity above an explicit smoothing threshold for bounded-plus-Gaussian residuals. With known support and oracle state pairs, the asymptotic covariance approaches the Cramér--Rao bound as smoothing vanishes and is strictly smaller than that of any Gaussian quasi-likelihood estimator under an explicit non-Gaussianity condition; for unknown sparse support we characterize the boundary limit, and we quantify the topology bias caused by residual-score mismatch. Third, we couple score-driven graph updates with an approximately fully adapted generative particle filter and prove, for bounded residuals under explicit excitation and forgetting conditions, a mean-square closed-loop bound with a step-size-independent small-gain condition. Synthetic and real-data experiments confirm these gains under non-Gaussian forcing.
♻ ☆ Robust stochastic first order methods in heavy-tailed noise via medoid mini-batch gradient sampling
Manojlo Vukovic, Dusan Jakovetic
We consider a first order stochastic optimization framework where, at each iteration, $K$ independent identically distributed (i.i.d.) data point samples are drawn, based on which stochastic gradients can be queried. We allow gradient noise to be heavy-tailed, with possibly infinite variances. For the considered heavy-tailed setting, many algorithmic variants have recently been proposed based on gradient clipping or other nonlinear operators (e.g., normalization) applied over noisy gradients. In this paper, we take an alternative approach and propose a novel gradient estimator. The core idea of proposed estimator is to split the $K$-sized data batch into $M$ distinct data chunks, form for each chunk the stochastic gradient, and select the stochastic gradient of the chunk that is medoid of gradients of all data-chunks. For a broad class of symmetric heavy-tailed gradient noise distributions, we show that the proposed estimator has a finite second moment even when the underlying gradient noise has an infinite second moment. For nonconvex objectives, this yields convergence to a neighborhood of zero in expected squared gradient norm at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$. We explicitly characterize the size of this neighborhood in terms of the noise and algorithm parameters. When the time horizon $T$ is known in advance, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ convergence rate. A diminishing step size achieves the same rate up to a logarithmic factor. Incorporating clipping or a more general nonlinear transformation yields high-probability convergence guarantees with the same rate up to logarithmic factors. Experimental results indicate that R-SGD-Mini and its clipped or nonlinear variant consistently perform favorably compared to SGD, clipped SGD, Nonlinear SGD and Median-of-Means based methods.
♻ ☆ Safety stock calculation with heteroscedastic, autocorrelated and heavy-tailed forecast errors, an adaptive parametric method.e
Luis Fernández-Palacios, Manuel Ceballos, Yolanda Muñoz-Ocaña
This study develops and validates an adaptive parametric method for sizing safety stock when forecast errors are autocorrelated, heteroscedastic, asymmetric, and heavy-tailed. Using four years of weekly forecasts from a fast-moving consumer goods company, the analysis identifies substantial positive autocorrelation, departures from normality, systematic forecast optimism, and heterogeneous relationships between forecast volume and error variance. The proposed method integrates several corrections into a modular, sequential safety-stock architecture. It constructs cumulative forecast errors over the operational action period, selects an SKU-specific parametric distribution, and determines a baseline protection point using an expected-shortage condition consistent with the target beta fill rate. A forecast-scaled module adjusts dispersion when error variance depends on forecast volume, while a Cycle-End Exposure safeguard limits within-cycle shortage risk when large replenishment lots increase exposure. Performance is evaluated through discrete-event simulation against the company's current method. The proposed method reduces average inventory by 9.9% and maximum inventory by 19.5%, with no statistically significant deterioration in beta fill rate or average stockout duration. The proportion of weeks without stockouts declines slightly, without evidence of more persistent or operationally severe shortages. The heteroscedasticity module provides selective benefits, with greater service improvements as variance dependence intensifies. The resulting framework is interpretable, adapts to SKU-specific statistical profiles, links distributional features to safety-stock outcomes, and can be integrated into existing ERP environments.
comment: 39 pages, 4 figures
♻ ☆ Soft projections for robust data-driven control
András Sasfi, Jaap Eising, Florian Dörfler
We consider data-based predictive control based on behavioral systems theory. In the linear setting this means that a system is described as a subspace of trajectories, and predictive control can be formulated using a projection onto the intersection of this behavior and a constraint set. Instead of learning the model, or subspace, we focus on determining this projection from data. Motivated by the use of regularization in data-enabled predictive control (DeePC), we introduce the use of soft projections, which approximate the true projector onto the behavior from noisy data. In the simplest case, these are equivalent to known regularized DeePC schemes, but they exhibit a number of benefits. First, we provide a bound on the approximation error consisting of a bias and a variance term that can be traded-off by the regularization weight. The derived bound is independent of the true system order, highlighting the benefit of soft projections compared to low-dimensional subspace estimates. Moreover, soft projections allow for intuitive generalizations, one of which we show has superior performance on a case study. Finally, we provide update formulas for soft projectors enabling the efficient adaptation of the proposed data-driven control methods in the case of streaming data.
♻ ☆ On Approximate Computation of Critical Points
Amir Ali Ahmadi, Georgina Hall
We show that computing even coarse approximations of critical points is intractable for simple classes of nonconvex functions. We first present a family of $n$-variate cubic polynomials with coefficients in $\{-1,0,1\}$ that have exact critical points but for which no polynomial-time algorithm can write down a $\sqrt{n}/4$-approximate critical point in its standard representation. We then show that computational hardness persists when an exact critical point has a short representation. More specifically, we prove that for every fixed $η>0$, unless P $=$ NP, no polynomial-time (or even pseudo-polynomial-time) algorithm can take an $n$-variate cubic polynomial with rational coefficients ${c_α}$ and return a point with gradient norm at most $(\max_α|c_α|)n^{1/2-η}$ whenever the polynomial has a critical point in $\{-1,0,1\}^n$. The algorithm may return an arbitrary point on all other inputs. Both results are essentially tight in their dependence on the dimension $n$. We also prove hardness results for lower-bounded functions and for an alternative notion of approximation, in which approximation is measured by distance to an exact critical point. Overall, our results stand in contrast to the commonly held belief that, in nonconvex optimization, approximate computation of critical points is a tractable task.
♻ ☆ Superlinear Convergence of Cyclic Gradient Methods with Historical Ritz Step Sizes
Ran Gu
The long-step Barzilai-Borwein (BB1) method, cyclic BB1, and limited memory steepest descent (LMSD) are special cases of limited memory steepest descent with retards (LMSDR), a family of methods using historical Ritz step sizes. We analyze a cyclic Ritz-step rule within LMSDR and a sampled LMSDR variant on strictly convex quadratics, seeking R-superlinear convergence guarantees in higher spectral dimensions. Let $n$ be the problem dimension and $m$ the history length. In exact arithmetic, we begin at $n=m+1$, the first dimension beyond the finite-termination case, and obtain an exact doubly exponential rate per gradient update for rolling reuse outside an explicit, possibly empty exceptional set. We extend this rate to nonempty open sets for $m+1\binom{n-1}{m}$. For any $n>m$, increasing $\ell$ eventually satisfies this condition. Geometrically spaced choices among finitely many sampling lists preserve the guarantee.
comment: 46 pages, 2 tables
♻ ☆ Computer-Aided Analysis of Gradient Descent under Generalized Smoothness
Valery Krivchenko
Under classical assumptions, performance of first-order methods has been studied quite comprehensively with the developed theoretical apparatus of modern optimization. The development of the Performance Estimation Problems (PEP) framework led to even deeper understanding and allowed computer-assisted derivation of exact worst-case guarantees. Unfortunately, PEP is not directly applicable for systems that involve SDP-incompatible constraints. This includes a wide range of non-standard assumptions, some of them are highly relevant for practice such as generalized smoothness. In this paper proposes an approach of utilizing template solutions to derive guarantees in settings that do not admit an equivalent SDP formulation of exact worst-case performance problem. The approach is showcased by studying the performance of the gradient descent method for convex functions that also satisfy $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness assumption. Despite the inherent conservatism of the approach, this paper improves and generalizes an existing convergence guarantee to showcase the approach.
comment: This is the extended version of the paper Krivchenko, V. O. (2026). Computer-Aided Analysis of Gradient Descent under Generalized Smoothness. Doklady Mathematics, 530(1), 5-13. The extended version is much more detailed. It contains expanded discussion of the approach as well as descriptions of PEP experiments
♻ ☆ Parameter-Free Dynamic Regret under Heavy-Tailed Noise
Vaneet Aggarwal
We study online convex optimization on a compact convex domain of diameter $D$ in which the learner observes, at each round, one stochastic subgradient and no loss values. The observations are conditionally unbiased, and the noise has an unconditional $p$-th moment at most $σ^p$ for an unknown $p\in(1,2]$; for $p<2$ its variance may be infinite. For a comparator sequence of path length $P_T$ we write $Λ_T=1+P_T/D$, and we show that the minimax expected dynamic regret is, up to numerical constants, \[ \min\Bigl\{GD\sqrt{TΛ_T}+σDT^{1/p}Λ_T^{(p-1)/p},\ GDT\Bigr\}, \] where $G$ bounds the subgradients. The lower bound holds on every compact convex domain of positive diameter. An algorithm that combines AdaGrad learners restarted at different frequencies through exponential weights with a data-dependent learning rate attains this rate for each fixed $p>1$, without knowing $G$, $σ$, $p$, or $P_T$: the constant of the first term is numerical, the constant of the second is $O(1+\log(p/(p-1)))$, and no logarithmic factor of $T$ appears. The analysis bounds the gradient energy separately on each restart block, which gives the exponent $(p-1)/p$ of $Λ_T$ in the noise term; a bound over the whole horizon gives the exponent $1/2$. Running the algorithm on epochs of doubling length removes the need to know $T$ at the cost of a factor $2+\sqrt2$. The appendices give a high-probability version and a synthetic study.
♻ ☆ Constrained Online Learning with Noisy Constraint Values
Vaneet Aggarwal
We study online convex optimization with time-varying constraints when the constraint values are observed only through noise. In each round the learner picks an action, pays a convex loss, and incurs a convex constraint value that should be nonpositive; it then receives unbiased estimates of the loss and constraint gradients, and an unbiased observation of the constraint value whose error has bounded variance. Performance is measured against the best fixed action in hindsight among those that satisfy every constraint, and violation by the largest total overspend over any interval of consecutive rounds, which we call budget violation. Our algorithm, LEDGER, has $O(\sqrt T)$ expected regret and $O(\sqrt{T\log T})$ expected budget violation over $T$ rounds, uses one projection per round, and needs no strictly feasible action. The logarithm cannot be removed: with Gaussian noise of fixed positive variance, every algorithm with $O(\sqrt T)$ worst-case regret has worst-case budget violation of order at least $\sqrt{T\log T}$, even if only the final total overspend is counted, and budget violation $O(\sqrt T)$ forces linear regret. When violation is instead the sum of the positive parts of the per-round constraint values (hard violation), no algorithm keeps both expected regret and expected hard violation sublinear if the noise distribution is not fixed, even for affine constraints. With a fixed and known Gaussian noise law of standard deviation $σ$, a worst-case lower bound of order $\min\{σ,1\}T(\log\log T/\log T)^2$ shows that regret and hard violation cannot both be made polynomially sublinear. Noisy constraint values therefore still allow a signed budget to be controlled, at the cost of a logarithmic factor, but not the hard violation.
♻ ☆ Optimal control of SDEs with merely measurable drift: an HJB approach
Kai Du, Qingmeng Wei
We investigate an optimal control problem for a diffusion whose drift and running cost are merely measurable in the state variable. Such low regularity rules out the use of Pontryagin's maximum principle and also invalidates the standard proof of the Bellman principle of optimality. We address these difficulties by analyzing the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. Working in a weak formulation of admissible controls, we first establish the state-equation solvability and Krylov estimates needed to make the control problem well defined. Using PDE techniques together with a policy iteration scheme, we prove that the HJB equation admits a unique strong solution, and this solution coincides with the value function of the control problem. Based on this identification, we establish a verification theorem and recover the Bellman optimality principle without imposing any additional smoothness assumptions. We further investigate a mollification scheme depending on a parameter $\varepsilon > 0$. It turns out that the smoothed value functions $V_{\varepsilon}$ may fail to converge to the original value function $V$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$, and we provide an explicit counterexample. To resolve this, we identify a structural condition on the control set. When the control set is countable, convergence $V_{\varepsilon} \to V$ holds locally uniformly.
♻ ☆ Large-time behavior and accuracy of the Mean-Field Ensemble Kalman Filter in the Linear Detectable Setting
Franca Hoffmann, Sangmin Park, Andrew M. Stuart
The ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF), originally developed in the geophysical sciences, is now widely used for state and parameter estimation problems in various domains of application, and in particular in high dimensional settings. It may be viewed as a robust, cheap-to-implement,alternative to the optimal, Bayesian, filter. However, despite its empirical successes, theoretical understanding of its properties, in relation to the optimal filter, is in its infancy. We contribute novel theoretical understanding, studying the behavior of the EnKF in the infinite particle number setting; this is known as the mean-field ensemble Kalman filter (MFEnKF). In the linear setting with Gaussian noise and Gaussian initial data the MFEnKF coincides with the optimal filter, which is characterized by the Kalman filter. Our focus in this paper will be the linear setting with Gaussian noise, but with non-Gaussian initial data. Under the assumptions of nondegeneracy of the signal noise and detectability of the signal-observation pair we make three specific contributions, studying both discrete and continuous formulations of the methodology. First, in discrete time, we derive the MFEnKF via a variational approximation of the Bayes update using a covariance-weighted optimal transport metric. Secondly, we use this metric to show that the MFEnKF is a strict contraction towards the subspace of Gaussian measures, giving explicit geometric rates in terms of the covariances, in both discrete and continuous time. Finally, in the continuous-time setting, we deduce a stable form of almost sure accuracy of the MFEnKF: given any pair of initial laws (satisfying mild conditions) for the MFEnKF and the optimal filter, the 2-Wasserstein distance between their distributions decays exponentially, for almost every observation path.
comment: 40 pages; minor revisions
♻ ☆ Uniform symmetric spectral finiteness of cones definable in o-minimal structures
Mitsuhiro Nishijima
Cone-constrained eigenvalues of a matrix are defined by a complementarity problem over a closed convex cone. We show that every closed convex cone that is definable in an o-minimal structure is uniformly symmetrically spectrally finite; that is, the cone spectra of symmetric matrices relative to the cone (the sets of their cone-constrained eigenvalues) have uniformly bounded cardinality. In particular, we derive explicit uniform bounds for semialgebraic cones, and the explicit uniform bound we obtain for a Löwner cone depends only on the order of the matrices in the cone. Using the uniform finiteness of cone spectra, we also show that the number of singular values relative to two closed convex cones definable in a common o-minimal structure is uniformly bounded. Finally, we provide a closed convex cone that is not definable in any o-minimal structure and for which the spectra of symmetric matrices are finite but have no uniform cardinality bound.
♻ ☆ Accelerating Sinkhorn for Entropy-Regularized Optimal Transport
Long Chen, Zeyi Xu
Entropy-regularized optimal transport is widely used to compare and align data distributions, but Sinkhorn can converge slowly at small regularization. We introduce Acc-Sinkhorn, a two-state Hessian-driven Nesterov iteration built on the dual mirror geometry of the row-reduced Sinkhorn map. The method combines momentum acceleration with an inexpensive descent safeguard, stable log-domain evaluation, and a prescribed homotopy schedule requiring neither line search nor curvature estimation. We prove global linear convergence of the safeguarded method, rule out consecutive restarts, and establish local accelerated convergence for fixed parameters without restarts through spectral analysis. Numerical comparisons with six methods on synthetic problems, color transfer, and bilingual word alignment show runtime speedups of up to about 26 over Sinkhorn, with additional rendering-accuracy comparisons for color transfer.
comment: 30 pages
♻ ☆ Optimal Algorithms for Nonlinear Estimation with Convex Models
Simon Foucart
A linear functional of an object from a convex symmetric set can be optimally estimated, in a worst-case sense, by a linear functional of observations made on the object. This well-known fact is extended here to a nonlinear setting: other simple functionals of the object can be optimally estimated by functionals of the observations that share a similar simple structure. This is established for the maximum of several linear functionals and even for the $\ell$th largest among them. Proving the latter requires an unusual variation of the analytical Hahn--Banach theorem. The existence results are accompanied by practical recipes relying on convex optimization to construct the desired functionals, thereby justifying the term of estimation algorithms.
♻ ☆ Splitting Compositions of Monotone Operators
Haoming Qu, Yefan Wu, Thomas Chaffey
Coupled convex optimisation equilibria and nonlinear circuits lead to inclusions of the form $0 \in Hx + A(Bx) - b$, where $A$ and $B$ are maximally monotone but the complete operator need not be monotone. We develop a one-parameter family of triangular warped-resolvent algorithms on product Hilbert spaces to solve such inclusions. Introducing $y \in Bx$ exposes a directed lift, and a composition-adapted kernel organizes each iteration into one evaluation of $H$ and one ordinary resolvent evaluation per factor block. A nonnegative multi-block gain matrix certifies a unique lifted solution, global linear convergence, and residual error bounds. An exact Schur reduction converts the $2n \times 2n$ condition into an equivalent $n \times n$ criterion. For nonpositive extrapolation, this criterion is necessary and sufficient to guarantee a unique fixed point and global linear convergence for all problems satisfying the given gain bounds. Minimum-gain estimates characterize its exact finite-stepsize feasibility boundary. A negative-coupling rotation family exhibits certified convergence when neither the original operator nor its specified lift admits a fixed positive-definite monotonicity metric. For a nonlinear periodic RLC circuit, we establish continuous-time nonmonotonicity and derive a computable convergence certificate. Our algorithm is demonstrated on a periodic circuit simulation problem.
comment: 23 pages, 4 figures. Revised manuscript with new multiport convergence results, a minimum-gain analysis of stepsize feasibility, and a nonlinear RLC circuit application
♻ ☆ Douglas--Rachford Algorithm with Relaxed Resolvents
Luis Briceño-Arias, Fernando Roldán, Adrien Taylor
In this paper we study the convergence of a generalization of the Douglas--Rachford algorithm for finding a zero of the sum of two maximally monotone operators, where reflected resolvents are extended to relaxed resolvents. This extension allows for different step sizes in the resolvents under cocoercivity. We show that the resulting method converges weakly when its parameters lie in a range determined by the cocoercivity constants, which reduces to the classical algorithm when these constants vanish. Our main results concern the cocoercive case when one of the operators is in addition strongly monotone, in which the composition is a strict contraction. For both monotone inclusions and convex minimization, we compute the contraction factor and its optimal parameters in closed form, and show that the resulting rates are tight. Whenever the second operator is cocoercive, the optimal rates are strictly smaller than the corresponding rates of forward-backward splitting and of the classical Peaceman--Rachford and Douglas--Rachford algorithms and, in convex minimization, than those of FISTA. All theoretical rates are corroborated by the numerical worst cases obtained via performance estimation.
♻ ☆ Sensitivity to Information Channel and Model Perturbations in Partially Observable Stochastic Control
Yunus Emre Demirci, Ali Devran Kara, Serdar Yüksel
Studying the stability of partially observed Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with respect to perturbations in the transition and observation kernels is a significant problem. While asymptotic robustness/stability results, as approximate transition kernels and/or measurement kernels converge to the true ones, have been previously reported, explicit bounds on value differences and mismatch costs have been limited in scope for POMDPs. The main technical contribution of this paper is a collection of explicit and uniform bounds on the distance between the filter kernels (that is, the kernels of the belief-MDP reduction) of two POMDPs, in the bounded-Lipschitz and Wasserstein metrics, in terms of the total variation and Wasserstein distances between their transition and measurement kernels; we also establish the sharpness of these bounds, demonstrate through counterexamples that the metrics employed cannot be weakened, and present verifiable conditions, stated directly in terms of the defining system functions, under which they apply. Building on these kernel proximity bounds, we show that control policies optimized for approximate models yield explicit performance guarantees when applied to the true model, under both discounted and average cost criteria. Two settings are treated separately: policy transfer, where the controller knows the true model and only the policy is designed for the approximate one, and model misspecification, where the controller also computes its beliefs with the approximate model. As a particular application, we consider the case where the state space and the measurement spaces are quantized to obtain finite models, and we obtain explicit error bounds which decay to zero as the approximations get finer. This provides explicit performance guarantees for model reduction in POMDPs.
♻ ☆ Initialization Stability and Convergence of Projected Langevin Dynamics
Qi Feng, Nathan Sauldubois, Xin Zhang
The entropic regularized optimal transport (EOT) plays a fundamental role in the computation of optimal transport. In \cite{CLP}, the authors proposed a gradient flow approach to EOT, and derived a projected Langevin diffusion that converges in distribution to the solution of EOT when initialized with a coupling between the two given marginals. In this paper, motivated by samplings of optimal couplings for EOT, we analyze the projected Langevin dynamics with arbitrary initial distribution, and prove that its long time behavior is the same as if it was initialized from a coupling.
♻ ☆ Global Exponential and Inverse Optimal Stabilization of a 3D Nonholonomic Vehicle in Spherical Coordinates IEEE Conference on Decision and Control
Kwang Hak Kim, Velimir Todorovski, Mamadou Diagne, Miroslav Krstic
For the 3D nonholonomic vehicle actuated in surge velocity, pitch rate, and yaw rate, we construct continuous time-invariant feedback laws that stabilize both the roll-free and roll-augmented kinematic models to a target position and orientation in spherical coordinates. The design uses a spherical coordinate transformation with a singular set of codimension two and measure zero. We first present a backstepping design that yields explicit unidirectional, cusp-free feedback laws and strict barrier control Lyapunov functions (CLFs). These establish global exponential stability in spherical coordinates with user-assigned decay rates, while ensuring bounded Cartesian trajectories and exponential convergence to the target, consistent with Brockett's obstruction. The barrier terms guarantee avoidance of the coordinate singularities away from the target. The strict CLFs are then used to develop families of asymptotically stabilizing inverse optimal feedback laws for both systems that minimize a meaningful infinite-horizon cost. These laws inherit infinite gain margins from driftlessness, respect user-defined input bounds through Legendre-Fenchel transformations, and are implementable with either bidirectional or unidirectional surge actuation. Two penalty choices are illustrated: a quadratic input penalty whose associated state running cost approaches a prescribed quadratic form, and an input-constraining penalty that enforces user-defined bounds. This paper lays the foundation for constructive stabilization of the 3D nonholonomic vehicle.

♻ ☆ Closing the Accuracy Gap in Stochastic First-Order Bilevel Optimization
Haihan Zhang, Wendao Wu, Chenheng Zhang, Yanyi Li, Chunyuan Zheng, Cong Fang, Haoxuan Li, Zhouchen Lin
We study the stochastic first-order complexity of smooth nonconvex-strongly-convex bilevel optimization with fresh, conditionally unbiased gradient samples of bounded variance. We assume globally $L$-Lipschitz gradients, bounded $f_y$, $μ$-strong convexity of the lower objective, and $ρ$-Lipschitz lower Hessian blocks. Let $κ=L/μ$, $\vartheta=ρ/μ$, and $χ=1+\vartheta$. For $κ\ge2$, $1\le\vartheta\leκ^2$, every initial-gap budget $Δ>0$, and $0<ε\le c\min\{L,\sqrt{LΔ}\}$, we establish $\mathsf{T}_{\mathrm{SFO}}(ε)=\widetildeΘ(Lχκ^{5/2}Δε^{-2}+Lκ^4σ_f^2Δε^{-4}+L^3\vartheta^2χκ^8σ_g^2Δε^{-6})$, where $σ_f^2$ and $σ_g^2$ are the upper- and lower-level variance budgets. The comparison assumes a finite lower-initialization certificate, holds uniformly over both nonnegative noise budgets, and uses an accuracy constant $c$ independent of conditioning. Three lower-bound families capture the deterministic, upper-noise, and lower-noise contributions. The bounds cover arbitrary randomized adaptive queries and terminal outputs under worst-case expected costs, even for conservative sample gradients. The upper bound combines accelerated frozen-linear-tilt solves with displacement-based reuse of the full upper gradient. An independently chosen base-chain length yields the uniform accuracy range, while a projection and homotopy argument separates undisclosed coordinates from a newly disclosed source, allowing $\vartheta/κ$ to grow without bound. The bounds match polynomial orders and noise transitions; exact logarithmic exponents and coarser accuracies remain open.

☆ Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action
Seongchan Kim, Soowon Son, Sangoh Kim, Hyunah Ko, Eunbeen Hong, Hyunkoo Lee, Sanghyun Lee, WonJun Moon, Kihong Kim, Dongyeon Son, Woongchan Nam, Seungryong Kim
Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.

☆ ACAP: Asynchronous Coding Agents for Efficient Robot Control
Zexin He, Rui Li, Yushi Lan, Chengkai Jin, Zhi Hou, Xingang Pan
Coding agents can construct and revise robot behavior during execution, but using one agent for the whole robot can delay otherwise independent work. We introduce Asynchronous Coding Agents as Policy (ACAP), an asynchronous framework that organizes one robot as a team of persistent agents. Each member reasons and acts for a configurable control group, such as an arm with its gripper or the torso and chassis, enabling asynchronous reasoning and execution. However, different robot components often have physical dependencies that require coordination. To address this challenge, ACAP introduces a hyper-agent that assigns tasks, coordinates dependencies, and dynamically allocates control between the lead and member agents. This allows independent work to progress concurrently while supporting tightly coupled manipulation when necessary. Across 72 real-world rollouts covering 25 task/platform settings, ACAP reduces task-balanced time cost by 28.2% compared with a single-agent Direct Policy, with improvements across Fully Parallel, Parallel-Sequential, and Collaborative tasks. Across all eight Collaborative settings, ACAP also achieves lower mean time cost than Fixed Delegation, where only member agents can control their assigned groups. An additional 90-rollout study shows lower mean 30-minute-capped time cost than Direct on all six tasks. We further demonstrate mobile manipulation using the same member interface for chassis and torso control. We present the framework and a real-world rollout dataset containing observations, generated programs, actions, and feedback to support research on how coding agents reason and act in the physical world.

☆ Embo-Harness: Towards Understanding Frontier-Model-as-Policy Harness
Xiao-Ming Wu, Kang Liao, Yuexiao Ma, Taolin Zhang, Mingqian Zhou, Nuo Chen, Ziming Li, Yihang Luo, Rui Li, Zhonghua Wu, Tianyu Xie, Xiawu Zheng, Zhongang Cai, Zhi Hou, Chen Change Loy
Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. We investigate four components of the robotic agentic loop, namely, prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use, and distill six empirical findings into a practical recipe. This recipe prioritizes interfaces that exploit the model's native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors, and identifies effective choices for action representation, chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement. On RoboLab-120, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3\% success rate, outperforming the strongest reported baseline by 26.2 percentage points. It also succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks. Beyond performance, controlled interventions indicate that the studied model depends more strongly on accurate spatial target estimation than on explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation. These results provide both a practical recipe for building strong frontier-model-as-policy harnesses and a clearer account of the capabilities that drive their performance.

☆ VITA-WAM: Manifold-Aligned World-Action Modeling for Real-Time Robot Control
Boqi Zhao, Dechen Gao, Hanchu Zhou, Hang Wang, Junshan Zhang
World action model (WAM) is a promising paradigm for visuomotor control by jointly modeling world dynamics and actions. Notably, existing WAMs often rely on large generative models and iterative sampling which incur substantial latency for action generation, limiting real-time deployment. In particular, there are two root causes of inefficiency in conventional flow matching or diffusion based action models in WAMs: 1) transporting uninformative Gaussian noise into precise actions necessitating multiple ODE steps, and 2) repeatedly injecting task context through expensive cross-attention modules. Our key insight is that jointly learning and aligning the source and action manifolds streamlines the transport between them, substantially accelerating action generation. Building on this insight, we introduce VITA-WAM, a WAM architecture with manifold-aligned flow-matching (VITA flow matching) that directly transports latent observation representations containing visual, language, and proprioceptive information into latent actions. More specifically, a flow latent alignment (FLA) mechanism is employed to facilitate manifold alignment between latent observation and action representations, enabling accurate generation with few ODE steps. The resulting architecture also eliminates costly attention for observation conditioning during repeated denoising steps. Notably, with a single ODE step, VITA-WAM outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 pp on LIBERO-Plus and by 1.65 pp on LIBERO, achieving these gains through the FLA objective without distillation, while inferring at 55.67~ms latency, a $2.10\times$ speedup compared to FastWAM.

☆ EmboEagle: An Efficient Agentic Embodied Framework for Long-horizon Robotic Manipulation
Fan Xu, Zhongtao Wang, Hao Wu, Yitong Zhu, Wenzhuo Ma, Long Li, Zhuohao Li, Zhisheng Chen, Rui Su, Kun Wang, Xian Wu, Wanli Ouyang
Long-horizon robotic manipulation demands reliable execution across interdependent stages, yet standalone World-Action Models (WAMs) suffer from compounding physical errors, while stateless Vision-Language Model (VLM) supervision incurs prohibitive chunkwise latency and lacks 3D spatial persistence. We present EmboEagle, a closed-loop agentic framework that unifies subtask-conditioned WAM control, latent-space adaptive supervision, and memory-guided geometric recovery. First, we adapt sequential WAMs via decoupled two-stage flow matching that preserves cross-stage visual history while calibrating truncated action supervision at subtask boundaries. Second, without an auxiliary vision encoder, we distill teacher intervention decisions into a lightweight routing gate driven solely by the WAM Action Expert's pre- and post-chunk latent transitions and subtask embeddings. Third, upon invocation, the VLM decouples diagnostic status from discrete routing actions and executes parameterized recovery primitives grounded in structured memory (initial references, active grasp bindings, and tool traces), followed by mandatory post-repair verification. Across RMBench and LIBERO-Mem, EmboEagle achieves 91.3\% and 90.6\% average success, surpassing the strongest baselines by 8.0 and 9.8 percentage points, while boosting real-world success over VoLoAgent under identical executor weights. Moreover, adaptive gating cuts VLM calls by 74.2\% versus chunkwise monitoring (91.3\% vs. 93.7\% success).
☆ WeaveVLA: 3D Relational Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models
Zien Wang, Yuhao Pan, Yunfeng Fan, Nan Cheng, Xin Xia, Wenchao Xu
Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for instruction-conditioned robot control, yet their understanding of task-relevant 3D relations and how these relations evolve during manipulation remains largely implicit. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{WeaveVLA}, a framework that enhances VLA action generation by explicitly modeling task-relevant relative 3D relations and maintaining relational context across observations. WeaveVLA employs a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to encode relative 3D relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references. Pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate geometric evidence across observations to maintain evolving spatial context. A learned-query readout summarizes the updated graph representations into compact relational tokens, which condition the action expert alongside the original vision-language context. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages spatial structure preservation. We instantiate WeaveVLA on StarVLA-GR00T and $π_{0.5}$, achieving over 98\% average success on LIBERO with both backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, WeaveVLA improves success from 74.9\% to 82.0\% and from 85.7\% to 87.8\%, respectively, with additional improvements on CALVIN D$\rightarrow$D. On three real-world tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T-based variant improves average success from 55.6\% to 70.0\% under standard conditions and from 33.3\% to 53.3\% under OOD perturbations, surpassing the $π_{0.5}$ baseline in both settings.

☆ RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
Yanzhe Chen, Zhijun Cao, Zechen Bai, Wenzheng Zeng, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Yiqi Lin, Guoqiang Liang, Xiaokang Liu, Ke Sun, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Mike Zheng Shou
Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.

☆ NoveltyGate: Novelty, Not Error, Decides Which VLA Prefix Tokens to Compute Exactly
Lemeng Qi
Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_{0.5}$ re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token's exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3--1.7$\times$ larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token's input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error--reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the $π_{0.5}$ prefix by up to 1.61$\times$, stays 2.7--2.9$\times$ closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.
☆ Real2Worlds2Real: Scaling Self-Improving Agentic Real2Sim2Real for Robot Manipulation
Jinzhong Gu, Jiakai Chen, Xinyi Cao, Yan Shen, Hangke Sui, Shutian Zheng, Xiang Xiao, Haoran Lu, Fan Xu, Lu Shi, Daochen Shi, Ruihua Zhang, Wei Zhan, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Ruihai Wu
Scaling robot manipulation learning remains challenging due to the high cost of collecting real-world interaction data. Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) offers a promising route by enabling policy learning in simulation grounded in real-world observations, yet scaling this paradigm across diverse tasks and physical interactions remains difficult. We introduce Real2Worlds2Real, a self-improving agentic framework that integrates scalable simulation-world construction with policy development. Given limited visual observations and task descriptions, its tool-orchestration harness constructs faithful digital twins and expands them into diverse, physically executable digital cousins. The agent adaptively selects tools and revisits construction decisions, using visual and execution feedback to refine geometry and physical behavior. Building on these worlds, the agent orchestrates policy development by coordinating data generation, policy learning, and refinement based on task requirements and simulation rollout feedback. Across both stages, the agent distills validated procedures into reusable skills that guide subsequent tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved world fidelity and successful real-world policy transfer, with performance gains from increasing world diversity and interaction-data volume. Skill reuse further improves world-building efficiency and long-horizon task success.
☆ Wrist-Camera Video Diffusion as Generalizable Robot Policies
Jingyuan Liu, Yongwei Chen, Yishan Yang, Zexin He, Xingang Pan, Zhi Hou
A generalist manipulation policy should perform new tasks, operate in unfamiliar scenes, and transfer skills across robot embodiments. We present Wrist Video Policy (WVP), a closed-loop manipulation framework that learns how manipulation unfolds through video prediction and recovers executable motion through geometric estimation. Our key idea is to represent robot motion through wrist-camera trajectories, which determine the corresponding end-effector poses through a fixed hand-eye transformation. We pair a video generator that predicts future wrist views with a pose estimator adapted from a pretrained 3D model to recover the corresponding camera trajectories. Model stitching maps the generator's predicted latents directly into the estimator's intermediate feature space, bypassing RGB decoding. This decomposition allows task knowledge to expand through broad human and robot video data while reusing geometric motion estimation across tasks and embodiments. The resulting pose estimator transfers across Franka Panda, PiPER-X, and Galaxea R1 Pro without further fine-tuning. Across tabletop and laundry-room settings, WVP generalizes to tasks ranging from precise grasping and inserting to handling deformable objects, achieving a success rate of over 50% in zero-shot out-of-distribution evaluations. Our project page is at https://wrist-video-policy.github.io.
☆ Completing analytical conversion scheme among DH, Hayati, CPC and POE models for manipulator calibration
Oleg Yu. Sumenkov, Danil D. Kulminskiy, Sergei V. Gusev
Building on Mooring's decomposition of the calibration procedure into four stages - modeling, measurement, identification, and correction - this paper investigates the role of analytical kinematic model conversion algorithms within the calibration framework and their potential to improve calibration performance. Four prominent and widely cited kinematic models: Denavit-Hartenberg (DH), Hayati (HAY), Complete and Parametrically Continuous (CPC), and Product of Exponentials (POE), - are considered. A systematic analysis of the existing conversion relationships reveals that, although most conversions among these models have already been established in the literature, a direct analytical conversion between POE and HAY, and CPC and HAY remains unavailable. Relying instead on a sequential combination of the existing POE-DH and DH-HAY conversions, for example, introduces several limitations. To address this gap, we develop a constructive analytical conversion between POE-HAY and HAY-CPC models based on Lie group theory, formally established through a set of lemmas and propositions. The proposed algorithms are illustrated using an RRRP SCARA robot and an RRHHHH Puma 560 manipulator. The direct POE-HAY conversion is compared with the sequential POE-DH-HAY approach, as well as HAY-CPC in terms of several relevant criteria, demonstrating the advantages of the proposed solution. Finally, we demonstrate the practical significance of the completed analytical conversion framework in an open-loop kinematic calibration experiment on an ABB IRB 1600 manipulator, using an API Radian EMSD3 Laser Tracker for measurements. The experimental results demonstrate that proper model selection combined with completed analytical conversion scheme directly improves calibration accuracy.
★ ReWeave: Emergent Physical Task Topologies for Embodied Harness Optimization and Cross-Task Meta-Distillation
Yicheng Xu, Wencan Jiang, Zihao Zhu, Keru Zhou, Chang Zhou, Li Liu, Maoqing Yao, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
Long-horizon embodied tasks involve physical dependencies that may only become clear through interaction. As task understanding deepens, past trials can reveal new information for adaptation and transfer. However, coarse progress feedback cannot identify which physical preconditions held, leaving search unguided, while task-specific optimization easily overfits to individual scenes, making cross-task transfer brittle. We introduce ReWeave, a framework that jointly optimizes an embodied agent harness and an emergent physical task topology from interaction without updating policy weights. Keeping execution policies and perception frozen, ReWeave co-optimizes coupled context, workflows, and control loops. As new evidence revises the topology, ReWeave reprojects past trials onto the updated task understanding, exposing retained progress, regressions, and bottlenecks that guide parent selection and search width. Across tasks, matching verified local mechanisms to unmet preconditions consolidates 72 specialist units into 44 reusable groups ($0.34\times$ full concatenation) within a compact shared harness capable of continual learning. ReWeave improves held-out success from 89.00% to 98.75% on LIBERO-PRO and from 25.50% to 58.25% on RoboDojo, while uncovering retained progress in 89% of 159 failed RoboDojo development trials and translating stronger offline reasoning into higher online performance. On eight unseen LIBERO-PRO tasks, the shared harness reaches 51.3% success versus 41.3% for direct distillation, rising to 75.0% after continual learning.

☆ SurgeCount: A Protocol-Guided Composition Harness for Bimanual Surgical Sponge Counting ML4H
Sung Eun Kim, Xiaoman Zhang, Xucheng Wang, Pranav Rajpurkar
We present SurgeCount, a system for auditable robotic surgical sponge counting that composes learned skills under a written procedural protocol. Retained sponges cause preventable harm, and surgical teams count every sponge before closure to reduce that risk. The robot repeatedly isolates one deformable sponge from a tangled pile and places it in the next numbered counting-tray slot, requiring handling of occluded grasp threads while preserving step order. We train one subtask-conditioned policy on eleven short skills and learn when each skill ends. At each learned boundary, a stateful vision-language model selects the next skill from an operator-authored specification of step order, visual verification, and recovery. This creates temporal commitment to each subtask and enables failures to be recovered by recomposing existing skills rather than using a dedicated recovery policy. We evaluate five methods across 100 real-robot trials using 20 matched layouts. SurgeCount fills 47 of 60 ordered slots and completes 12 of 20 procedures, compared with 27 of 60 and 3 of 20 for the strongest of four end-to-end policies trained on the same data. Replacing the detailed protocol prompt with a minimal prompt reduces performance to 29 of 60 slots and 5 of 20 completed procedures. These results show that long-horizon performance depends not only on visuomotor capacity, but also on how learned skills are committed, verified, and composed. This tabletop proof of concept motivates further evaluation of protocol-guided robotic sponge counting in clinically representative settings.

☆ RoboUniverse-10K: Toward the Scaling Era of Agentic Robotics via Real-to-Sim Environments
Jinkun Liu, Yingze Wang, Situ Wang, Deyao Hong, Mingju Gao, Wenyi Li, Yizhe Chi, Youjie Zheng, Kaisen Yang, Xiangyang Wang, Bingxiang He, Yuxin Zuo, Boyuan Chen, Yue Chen, Cheng Qian, Tianxing Chen, Huichi Zhou, Huaxiu Yao, Hao Tang, Hao Zhou, Ya-Qin Zhang, Calvin Xiao, Tiga Altman, Huan-ang Gao
Agentic Robotics, in which foundation models act as coding agents to control robots through executable programs, has emerged as a compelling paradigm for embodied intelligence. Yet unlike software engineering, where massive executable environments power post-training, robotics remains constrained by small, manual benchmarks and in-distribution evaluation. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboUniverse-10K, 10,807 interactive, resettable, and verifiable physics environments built from real-world videos via an automated Real2Sim and quality assurance pipeline. Each runs in an isolated, Harbor-compatible harness that hides privileged states and grading logic to mirror real-world sensing. From the same pipeline, we hold out 500 unseen tasks to establish RoboUniverse-Verified, an expert-verified zero-shot benchmark. Evaluating 11 closed- and open-source models reveals a huge gap: frontier models reach 85.8\% success, while open-source baselines lag at 2.6\% to 10.0\%, bottlenecked by low-level grasping, deformable-object manipulation, and post-contact physical control. Finally, we collect about 17K multi-turn trajectories totaling 0.79B tokens with GPT-6 Astra and perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, yielding RoboUniverse-35B-A3B. Our model achieves substantial zero-shot gains on RoboUniverse-Verified, lifting the success rate from 0.8\% to 21.2\%, while achieving zero-shot task completions across LIBERO-MAX, RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0, and a real Franka arm. We open-source the RL-ready environments and model to lay the foundation for large-scale reinforcement learning in Agentic Robotics.

☆ Generalizing Agentic Robotics via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
Xinxin Liu, Anh Dao, Wenrui Bao, Rafid Ahmed, Bingxin Xu, Ming Li, Chen Chen, Yuzhang Shang
Building general-purpose robots is a central goal in robotics. Agentic robotics pursues this goal with planners that control robots through tool calls. However, existing methods either rely on proprietary models accessed through APIs, which incur high costs and latency, or post-train a planner with reinforcement learning (RL) in a single domain, requiring a separate specialist for each domain with incompatible tools. In large language model (LLM) post-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) has been used to consolidate domain specialists into a single generalist. Yet whether MOPD can build a generalist planner for agentic robotics, how well it performs, and how it compares with other consolidation methods remain unexplored. In this paper, we systematically study these questions: we introduce Robo-MOPD, which trains a single student on closed-loop rollouts in simulation under token-level supervision from matching frozen specialists, and compare it with weight merging, off-policy specialist supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-domain online RL. Experiments on LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 show that a single 9B Robo-MOPD planner reaches 72.9% and 44.8% success (58.9% average), surpassing all consolidated baselines in average success and both 9B specialists on their respective benchmarks. Robo-MOPD excels on long-horizon tasks, outperforming multi-domain online RL by 13.0 percentage points on LIBERO-10.
☆ WorldLeague: Benchmarking Physical Agency
Xinyang Zhou, Qi Li, Xinchao Wang
AI systems can now operate Blender, follow instructions in complex video games, and manipulate objects with robot arms. What range of physical goals can today's AI systems achieve autonomously? Answering this question requires testing systems on tasks that demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action. We introduce \textbf{WorldLeague}, a benchmark that compares AI systems on a common set of \textbf{60 simulated robot tasks} by measuring progress toward each task's physical goal from the robot's trajectory. Robots explore scenes to gather evidence in \textbf{WorldSeek}, rearrange objects in \textbf{WorldShape}, and adapt to changes in \textbf{WorldShift}. Tying these goals to a single control interface limits which AI systems can be compared. In WorldLeague, vision-language models (VLMs) choose targets and motions, while vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) use their native controls. For each of six capability dimensions, we measure how much progress a system makes toward its goals (Interactive Score) and how often it achieves them (physical success rate). Together, these measures form the system's \emph{Physical Agency Profile}. Among 13 representative AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 achieves 13 of the 60 goals and earns the highest mean Interactive Score (28.58/100). Fable leads in four dimensions, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra tie for first on rule-following tasks. Even when VLMs answer every final question correctly, they receive an Interactive Score of zero in 71.8\% of those episodes. WorldLeague gives Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI a shared basis for comparing what AI systems achieve autonomously, from partial progress toward a physical goal to full goal completion. Project Webpage: https://xyangzhou.github.io/WorldLeague

Mishuo Han, Zhixuan Liang, Zhaoyuan Wan, Wendi Chen, Jiarui Chen, Xinkai Wang, Yue Ma, Yu Zhou, Junting Chen, Yao Mu, Jun Lv, Chuan Wen, Cewu Lu
Robotic manipulation policies can improve action prediction by anticipating how objects move and how their spatial relationships change. World Action Models (WAMs) learn to predict future visual observations, but their training objectives typically leave the underlying 3D geometric transitions implicit. To alleviate this problem, we introduce Foresight Forcing ($\mathcal{F}^{2}$), a WAM that learns a spatial transition representation from changes in a pretrained 3D feature space. During training, a frozen 3D foundation model extracts patch-wise feature differences from aligned current and future observations that provide dense supervision for geometry-aware feature transitions. We distill these targets into spatial transition queries, which are progressively refined from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state, and use them alongside current visual features to generate actions. At deployment, the policy predicts the queries without future observations or the 3D teacher. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, including 95.01% average success on RoboTwin2.0 Full. On six real-world manipulation tasks, $\mathcal{F}^{2}$ achieves a mean task score of 85.8%.

☆ SayDo: Benchmarking the Safety of Frontier Models from Chat to Closed-Loop Robot Control
Benjamin Alt
Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level robot controllers, yet their safety is evaluated almost entirely in text. We introduce SayDo, a benchmark that assesses the propensity of frontier models to cause harm in embodied contexts. SayDo comprises eleven laboratory and household tasks that pair a benign instruction with a hazard latent in the scene. Tasks are implemented in six settings along an embodiment gradient, from chat questions about an imagined robot to closed-loop control of a simulated robot arm. Benign controls, safe-alternative variants and scripted operator pushback complement each task. Across six open- and closed-weight VLMs and 11,480 episodes, hazardous-action rates rise from 14% in chat to 47% in the simulator, and from 2% to 80% for the most affected model. The increase is largely driven by open-weight models. We find that models flag hazards before acting in 73% of unsafe episodes and give way to pushback about twice as often when controlling robots as in chat. The safest models also show signs of overcaution on benign controls. Safety evaluations run in text therefore do not predict the safety behavior of the same models when used as robot controllers.

Personalization of powered prosthesis control to individual user needs remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, policy iteration with constraint embedded (PICE), a reinforcement learning (RL) tuning approach, has been developed and validated. This feasibility study investigated whether the developed approach can personalize a commercial powered knee prosthesis under clinically realistic conditions. To reduce the time for personalization, tuning was initialized with a policy learned offline from one non-disabled participant walking on a treadmill and was then applied to three other non-disabled participants walking with the knee through a bypass adapter on a 5-meter walkway. All participants reached the goal within 8-18 tuning steps (1.7-4.2 minutes of walking), reducing the knee-kinematic feature error by 64-90% on average. These results support the feasibility of implementing the RL-based tuning approach in clinically realistic conditions with space and equipment constraints.

☆ CoSel: Cooperation as Selection for End-to-End Driving
Yiping Li, Haohua Que, Zhipeng Bao, Wenjie Zhao, Qianwen Li
Cooperative driving can extend a vehicle's awareness beyond its own sensors, but existing cooperative end-to-end methods inject shared information into the planner and rely on cooperative driving demonstrations to learn how to use it. The moments in which shared information should change a driving decision are rare in such data, providing limited supervision for learning this behavior. We argue that cooperation need not be learned by the planner. Instead, reacting to shared information requires predicting how surrounding agents will move and selecting a response from the candidate trajectories of an ego planner. We introduce CoSel, a cooperation-as-selection framework that leaves the planner and its ego-only input unchanged. A separately trained cooperative predictor uses observations from the ego vehicle, roadside units, and connected automated vehicles to predict surrounding agents and their future motion. CoSel evaluates the planner's candidate trajectories against these predictions, preserves the planner's choice when it remains safe, and selects the closest safe alternative when shared information reveals additional risk. Each safety intervention is traceable to the shared evidence that triggers it. In closed-loop evaluation, CoSel achieves a driving score of 70.7 on V2Xverse, outperforming the best compared cooperative method by 7.5 points, and the highest average driving score of 85.8 on MDrive. Under missing ego detections, the collision count of CoSel increases only from 17 to 19 in 72 scenarios, compared with 19 to 32 for an existing cooperative end-to-end model.

☆ DexLatentWorld: 3D Cross-Embodiment Latent Action World Models for Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation
Vinay Udit Mohan, Xuchuan Huang, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.

☆ GlanceNav: Efficient Vision-and-Language Navigation with Streaming Memory and Counterfactual Rewind
Anh Dao, Quan-Dung Pham, Danh Vinh Le, Tuyen Pham Le, Quan Nguyen, Yuzhang Shang
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong policies for vision-and-language navigation (VLN). However, most of them encode a sample of past frames again at every decision and are trained on isolated decisions, so computation is redundant and the usable history is short. They also learn from their own mistakes through outcome rewards that give one scalar to a whole episode. We ask whether a navigator can encode each frame only once, at a constant cost per step, and still remember what matters and learn efficiently from its mistakes. We present GlanceNav, a streaming navigator built on a hybrid MLLM. Its Gated DeltaNet layers carry a recurrent state through the whole episode, while its attention layers keep a short window of recent observations and a small bank of keyframes, selected by how much each frame changes the recurrent state. This constant-size memory keeps the cost per step fixed and allows training on whole episodes with the same memory as at inference. Because the entire memory can also be copied in constant time, we further propose Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe), a reinforcement learning stage that rewinds a drifting rollout to its closest approach to the goal, lets an expert correct a few actions, and credits decisions by the resulting change in outcome. Trained only on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits, with 1,000 instructions for reinforcement learning, a 4B GlanceNav reaches success rates of 71.9% and 73.6% on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen. On R2R-CE, it outperforms the strongest previous single-RGB method trained without external data by 9.1 points, while running at 104 ms per step.
☆ World Models as Native Latent Action Models
Qinyue Li, Weijie Qiao, Qingyi Tao, Zerui Gong, Zhe Yang, Quanzhou Li, Taolin Zhang, Jinglin He, Zhonghua Wu, Chen Change Loy
Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.

Zhen Xu, Hao-Run Cai, Heng-Zhuang Li, Si-Yang Liu, Jun-Peng Jiang, Han-Jia Ye
