♻ ☆ Contextual Distributionally Robust Optimization with Causal and Continuous Structure
Fenglin Zhang, Jie Wang
WWe propose a framework for contextual distributionally robust optimization (DRO) that considers the causal and continuous structure of the underlying distribution, and we develop interpretable and tractable decision rules. We first introduce the causal Sinkhorn discrepancy (CSD), an entropy-regularized causal Wasserstein distance that encourages continuous transport plans while preserving causal consistency. We then formulate a contextual DRO model with a CSD-based ambiguity set, termed Causal Sinkhorn DRO (Causal-SDRO), and derive its strong dual reformulation, where the worst-case distribution is characterized as a mixture of Gibbs distributions. To obtain an (infinite-dimensional) optimal policy, we propose a soft regression forest (SRF) decision rule: it preserves the interpretability of classical decision trees while being fully parametric, differentiable, and Lipschitz-smooth, enabling intrinsic interpretation from both global and local perspectives. To solve Causal-SDRO with parametric decision rules, we develop an efficient stochastic compositional gradient algorithm that converges to an $\varepsilon$-stationary point with $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ iteration complexity and $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-5})$ sample complexity. Finally, numerical results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance and interpretability of our method.
♻ ☆ AI for Games in the Foundation Model Era
Meng Luo, Yanlin Li, Hao Li, Hongzhan Lin, Pengfei Zhou, Tianjie Ju, Ran Zhang, Yeying Jin, Mong-Li Lee, Wynne Hsu
Foundation models, alongside advances in learned game-world models, are reshaping AI across the game lifecycle. Beyond playing games, recent systems model players and game dynamics, support design and development, adapt player-facing experiences at runtime, and evaluate resulting artifacts. Yet these directions have evolved largely separately, obscuring which capabilities transfer across settings and which remain tied to particular games, engines, interfaces, or player populations. We organize the literature into six roles according to the immediate use of AI output: playing and acting; modeling players and games; designing games; building and maintaining games; generating and adapting at runtime; and testing and evaluating games. For each role, we examine what structure is supplied by the game or workflow, what AI learns or produces, which capabilities and artifacts transfer across settings and roles, and what evidence supports the claims. We identify cross-role connections: trajectories train world models, learned environments provide experience for agents, design specifications drive executable implementations, and play or testing feedback guides revision. Evaluation is most standardized for bounded game playing and selected learned environments, while persistent state in learned worlds, repeated software revision, validated player modeling, sustained runtime adaptation, and representative automated testing remain less established. The central challenge is to reuse or transfer outputs and capabilities across roles while re-establishing evidence for effectiveness in the game-specific contexts where they are used.

♻ ☆ Fixed-Point Reasoners: Stable and Adaptive Deep Looped Transformers NeurIPS 2026
Sajad Movahedi, Vera Milovanović, Shlomo Libo Feigin, Alexander Theus, Thomas Hofmann, Valentina Boeva, T. Konstantin Rusch, Antonio Orvieto
Looped architectures provide an inductive bias toward learning step-by-step procedures for tasks that require compositional reasoning. Increasing the effective layers of looped architectures can improve their reasoning capabilities. Similar to deep architectures, looped architectures are prone to a signal propagation problem induced by depth as the halting decision is postponed. In this paper, we address the signal propagation issue by using pre-norm layers and residual scaling. By improving signal propagation, we achieve competitive performance without hierarchical looping, resulting in a simpler architecture than previous state-of-the-art models evaluated on puzzle reasoning tasks. Building on these modifications, we propose FPRM: a Transformer-based Fixed-Point Reasoning Model that uses fixed-point convergence as an end-to-end halting mechanism in a looped architecture. We show that fixed-point halting allows FPRM to adapt its compute to the difficulty of the task. FPRM proves effective on common reasoning benchmarks, namely sudoku, maze, state-tracking and ARC-AGI.

♻ ☆ Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge
Guilherme Guedes, Marco P. Apolinario, Charlotte Frenkel
Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.
♻ ☆ Rhythm-TTS: High-Fidelity Shortcut Latent Modeling and Probabilistic Rhythm Generation for Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech EACL
Hieu-Nghia Huynh-Nguyen, Ngoc-Son Nguyen, Long-Khanh Pham, Huynh Nguyen Dang, Huy Tien Nguyen, Van Nguyen
Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) systems are commonly built on either discrete codec tokens or continuous acoustic representations. Discrete-token models benefit from stable sequence modeling and explicit speech factorization, but they ultimately synthesize speech through codebook lookup and codeword composition, which can accumulate errors and impose a quality ceiling on naturalness and speaker similarity. Continuous-representation models can generate fine-grained speech latents directly, but often require heavier in-context modeling and less explicit alignment. This paper presents Rhythm-TTS, a shortcut zero-shot TTS framework that combines the factorizability of discrete codec tokens with the fidelity of continuous latent generation. Instead of using predicted codec tokens as the final acoustic representation, Rhythm-TTS uses them as a semantic-acoustic prior and directly generates holistic continuous speech latents with flow matching, bypassing the discrete-to-latent reconstruction path at inference time. We further address an underexplored dimension of speech naturalness: rhythm diversity across multiple synthesis runs. Motivated by the hypothesis that rhythm variation is largely governed by phoneme duration changes and the occurrence of silent pauses, we introduce probabilistic Duration and Silence Generators to sample dynamic pacing patterns before acoustic generation. Experiments on zero-shot TTS benchmarks evaluate intelligibility, naturalness, speaker similarity, efficiency, and run-to-run rhythm diversity, showing that the proposed shortcut latent modeling and probabilistic rhythm generation improve the fidelity and temporal naturalness of non-autoregressive zero-shot TTS. Code and audio samples are available at our demo page https://rhythm-tts.github.io.

♻ ☆ SpikeSTAG: A Dendritic Compartmental Spiking Graph Network for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
Bang Hu, Changze Lv, Junyi Wang, Mingjie Li, Xiaoqing Zheng, Fan Zhang, Wei Cao
Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a distinctive paradigm for temporal modeling through their intrinsic membrane potential dynamics. However, existing SNN-based forecasting methods focus exclusively on temporal processing, lacking mechanisms to capture spatial dependencies among variables. To bridge this gap, we propose SpikeSTAG, a neuromorphic spatiotemporal architecture that integrates graph-based spatial reasoning into spike-driven temporal computation. Central to our approach is the Dendritic Graph Module, which reinterprets spectral graph convolutions as biological dendritic integration --- coupling multi-scale spatial aggregation with the temporal dynamics of spiking neurons within a single computational unit. To adaptively fuse the resulting spatial and temporal representations, we further introduce a Dual-Stream Integration Module that employs competitive gating and coincidence-based amplification, selectively enhancing consistent spatiotemporal patterns while suppressing conflicting noise. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SpikeSTAG establishes a new state-of-the-art among SNN-based models and surpasses representative ANN baselines, while reducing theoretical energy consumption by approximately 66.7\% compared to Transformer architectures.

♻ ☆ ASCII Attack: Recontextualising Harmful Requests as Artistic Critique in Large Language Models

Safety alignment trains large language models (LLMs) to refuse harmful requests. However, a request can keep its operational content and still change how the model interprets it, and refusal training covers such "recontextualised" requests only weakly. To study this gap, we propose the ASCII Attack, a single-turn black-box jailbreak. It embeds a fully legible harmful request in an assembly of ASCII-art characters, presents it as artwork, and asks the model for "artistic feedback". ArtPrompt masks a sensitive word that the model must decode. In contrast, the ASCII Attack hides nothing and changes only the social frame of the request. In order to separate the effect of this frame from topic, model and decoding effects, we pair every framed prompt with a matched direct-question control on the same request. The control also omits the scene description and the missing-information list, so the contrast measures the framing bundle rather than the frame alone. Across eleven models and eight harm topics, the JailbreakBench classifier judges 62% of framed prompts harmful against 42% of their controls. With a single query, the ASCII Attack matches or exceeds ArtPrompt and DeepInception under four of five harm judges. We further show that the effect tracks the model more than the topic and does not fall with scale, which is consistent with mismatched generalisation.

♻ ☆ Neurosymbolic Learning for Inference-Time Argumentation NeurIPS 2026
Gabriel Freedman, Adam Dejl, Adam Gould, Mansi, Lihu Chen, Junqi Jiang, Francesca Toni
Claim verification is an important problem in high-stakes settings, including health and finance. When information underpinning claims is incomplete or conflicting, uncertain answers may be more appropriate than binary true or false classifications. In all cases, faithful explanations of the considerations determining the final verdict are crucial. We introduce inference-time argumentation (ITA), a trainable neurosymbolic framework for ternary claim verification in which a formal argumentation semantics giving the strength of claims and arguments is used both (i) to guide LLM training as models learn to generate arguments for and against claims and assign them base scores (representing intrinsic strengths) and (ii) to compute ternary (true/false/uncertain) predictions from generated, scored arguments. As a result, at training time, argument generation and scoring can be optimised according to the quality of the induced argumentative predictions. Moreover, at inference time, the final prediction is faithful, by construction, to the arguments and scores determining the verdict, rather than being justified by a potentially unfaithful post-hoc reasoning trace as in conventional reasoning models. We finally show that, on two datasets for ternary claim verification, ITA improves upon argumentative baselines and can perform competitively against non-argumentative direct-prediction baselines, while providing verdicts that are computed deterministically from explicit, inspectable argumentative structures. Our code, models and data are available at https://github.com/CLArg-group/inference-time-argumentation.

♻ ☆ Non-Expanding Gated Continued Fraction Architecture for Feedforward Layers in Language Models NeurIPS 2026
Amit Dhurandhar, Vijil Chenthamarakshan, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy, Dennis Wei, Rahul Nair
Recent work has shown that continued fraction inspired neural architectures (CoFrGeNets) can be highly parameter efficient yet performant for language modeling. In this work, we revisit continued fraction-based channel mixing with the goal of improving its performance and simplifying integration into standard pre-training protocols for language models. We achieve this by two simple yet critical contributions: i) we propose a novel non-expanding gated continued fraction inspired architectural component to replace feedforward layers in established language model architectures that may use vanilla multilayer perceptrons or gated linear units or (vanilla/gated) experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) type architectures. ii) We propose a way to re-implement divisions -- the non-linearity in these architectures -- in terms of logarithms and exponentials. By experimenting on different language modeling architectures such as GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2 and (nano) Llama-MoE we find that our proposed architecture performs similarly or significantly better than the continued fraction architecture proposed in prior work along with having higher throughput. In addition, our re-implementation of divisions makes training of deeper CoFrGeNets stable without the need for incremental training which was proposed in prior work as a means to stabilize training, but added notable complexity to existing large language model training implementations. Code is available at http://github.com/IBM/CoFrNets
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ Bring Back Language to Actions: Restoring VLM capabilities in VLA Models via Parameter Merging EACL 2027
Mohamed Salim Aissi, Olivier Sigaud, Laure Soulier, Nicolas Thome
Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector (the difference between VLA and VLM weights) and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.
comment: Accept at EACL 2027 (Main)
♻ ☆ Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models

We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens and 398 s for 16,384 tokens, and covers Qwen3-32B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B (4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s). A proof costs 41 to 50 times the serving time, or 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. On WikiText-2, F_O's greedy token matches the BF16 model's at 86.3% of positions; on Qwen3, F_O is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. A verifier with a compiled core checks a proof on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. In the random-oracle model, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2^-103. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models. Code: https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable
♻ ☆ What Frame-Level Labels Can and Cannot Do for Small-UAV Point Detection in Thermal Video
Wonbin Son, Gyumum Choi, Junil Seo, Hyungjoon Kim
The growing use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has increased the importance of image-based UAV detection. Learning-based detectors are trained on imagery and annotations, with annotation type determining the information available during training. We focus on learning localization from frame-level target presence/absence labels when sensor or scene changes make spatial annotations for additional training burdensome. We analyze the detection capability, learning behavior, and potential applications of an existing architecture for point detection of small UAVs, trained with presence/absence labels and requiring no external detector. The architecture freezes spatial features learned through classification and trains a readout with the same frame labels to produce spatial score maps and point detections. On two thermal infrared datasets, CST Anti-UAV and Anti-UAV410, we evaluate localization hit rates and detection rates under false-alarm constraints, analyze the effects of training stages, label allocation, synthesis, and model configuration, and compare with bounding-box detectors. We also explore potential applications on Airborne Object Tracking (AOT) using its visible-light imagery and frame labels. Classification training strengthened target-related spatial responses, while readout training helped extract them consistently. Distributing similar label counts across more videos yielded higher localization hit rates, while synthesis effects varied by dataset and evaluation criterion. Higher localization hit rates did not always improve detection under false-alarm constraints, and failures remained when target signals were weak relative to background variation and under cross-dataset transfer. These findings provide guidance on label allocation, spatial representations and readouts, synthesis, and false-alarm control.
♻ ☆ HyperCLOVA X 32B Think
NAVER Cloud HyperCLOVA X Team
In this report, we present HyperCLOVA X 32B Think, a vision-language model designed with particular emphasis on reasoning within the Korean linguistic and cultural context, as well as agentic ability. HyperCLOVA X 32B Think is pre-trained with a strong focus on reasoning capabilities and subsequently post-trained to support multimodal understanding, enhanced reasoning, agentic behaviors, and alignment with human preferences. Experimental evaluations against comparably sized models demonstrate that our model achieves strong performance on Korean text-to-text and vision-to-text benchmarks, as well as on agent-oriented evaluation tasks. By open-sourcing HyperCLOVA X 32B Think, we aim to support broader adoption and facilitate further research and innovation across both academic and industrial communities.
comment: Technical Report
♻ ☆ HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni
NAVER Cloud HyperCLOVA X Team
In this report, we present HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni, the first any-to-any omnimodal model in the HyperCLOVA X family that supports text, audio, and vision as both inputs and outputs. By consolidating multimodal understanding and generation into a single model rather than separate modality-specific pipelines, HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni serves as an 8B-scale omni-pathfinding point toward practical any-to-any omni assistants. At a high level, the model unifies modalities through a shared next-token prediction interface over an interleaved multimodal sequence, while vision and audio encoders inject continuous embeddings for fine-grained understanding and grounding. Empirical evaluations demonstrate competitive performance against comparably sized models across diverse input-output combinations spanning text, audio, and vision, in both Korean and English. We anticipate that the open-weight release of HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni will support a wide range of research and deployment scenarios.

Optimization and Control 70
☆ A Unified View of Operator Splitting and Interior-Point Methods
Gabriel Berk Pereira, Paul J. Goulart
First-order splitting and interior-point methods offer contrasting computational trade-offs for convex conic quadratic programs, yet their linear systems look remarkably similar. We make this connection precise through the Moreau slack, an unconstrained variable from which multipliers and (ordinary) slacks satisfying exact or barrier-perturbed complementarity are recovered. The remaining feasibility equations define a unified residual whose roots are KKT points at zero barrier parameter and central-path points at positive barrier parameter. Applying splitting to this residual yields projection methods at zero barrier parameter and barrier splitting at positive parameter; Newton's method in the latter setting gives an implicit interior-point method. At fixed positive barrier parameter, matching the splitting metric to current barrier curvature equalises the primal variable corrections under the same regularisation and leaves a factor of two between the Moreau-slack corrections. With metrics frozen at a barrier solution, local analysis identifies when doubling improves (local) convergence and when the primal solve remains the bottleneck. Metric choices that simplify linear solves (eg make them diagonal) become Newton regularisations, exposing a shared convergence cost associated with computational convenience. Finally, a computable defect in the regularised Newton equations gives an accuracy-based criterion for reusing a splitting factorisation.
comment: 16 pages
☆ Black-Box Comparator-Adaptive Network Regret
Tomas Ortega, Hamid Jafarkhani
We study comparator-adaptive decentralized online learning with network regret, which evaluates each node's prediction on the loss of every node in the network. We show that existing gossip-based algorithms are fundamentally limited for this task, and cannot achieve sublinear network regret with only one gossip step per decision round. To prove this, we construct a two-node counterexample, which shows that gossip-based algorithms can produce exponential regret despite bounded disagreement, resolving a previously open question in the literature. We then introduce a black-box reduction, which uses local learners with sublinear comparator-adaptive regret to obtain sublinear comparator-adaptive network regret. Each node exchanges predictions with its neighbors once per decision round, and a universal choice of edge weights works on every connected undirected graph without graph preprocessing. We also characterize admissible edge weights and show how weights adapted to the graph improve the regret bound. For example, for the complete graph, this improvement is quadratic in the number of nodes. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data illustrate the counterexamples we propose and compare the reduction with decentralized baselines.
☆ Self-Supervised Learning for Soft-Constrained AC-OPF in Multiphase Distribution Systems

This paper presents a self-supervised learning framework for fast, soft-constrained AC optimal power flow (OPF) in unbalanced multiphase distribution systems. The soft AC-OPF objective balances operating cost, renewable energy curtailment, and penalties for violating operating limits. A neural network predicts distributed energy resource (DER) setpoints conditioned on operating conditions, switch configurations, and objective weights. The predicted setpoints are then processed through a DER projection and differentiable AC power flow to enforce device limits and network equalities. The framework is trained by directly minimizing the AC-OPF objective, without optimal-solution labels. Experiments on 123-, 240-, and 906-bus systems yield mean objective gaps of 0.32%, 0.92%, and 0.56%, respectively, relative to IPOPT, across wide operating ranges. Across these systems and the evaluated high-load/low-generation and low-load/high-generation scenarios, the largest mean gap is 1.04%, with mean speedups of 58-5272 times relative to IPOPT.

☆ Congestion-Aware Adaptive Routing for LLM Classification
Yuan Guo, Stefanus Jasin, Chen-An Lin
Organizations use large language models (LLMs) to classify jobs that differ in uncertainty and the cost of errors. Querying additional models may improve accuracy, but it also incurs fees and increases congestion at shared servers. We study congestion-aware adaptive routing (CAAR) policies that adapt model selection and stopping decisions to observed outputs while accounting for the steady-state congestion they generate. The objective is to minimize the long-run average cost of misclassification penalties, query fees, and holding costs. We can represent CAAR policies as a mixture of decision trees, and derive exact holding costs for first-come-first-served servers with exponential service times and processor-sharing servers with general service times. We formulate a convex optimization problem with unique optimal model loads. Congestion prices capture the marginal system-wide holding costs of additional queries and guide routing and stopping decisions through a Bayesian dynamic program. We characterize optimal stopping decisions and identify models whose information does not justify their cost. A column-generation algorithm computes optimal CAAR policies and provides an explicit optimality-gap bound. We also bound the additional cost of limiting cascade depth relative to full-depth CAAR. Finally, under a common query-depth limit, cascades with a predetermined model order can be arbitrarily more costly than optimal CAAR, even when the order is randomized and stopping decisions adapt to observed outputs. Numerical experiments distinguish the benefits of adaptive model selection and congestion-aware design.
☆ Connected Lie groups with a left-invariant intrinsic chronometer

In this paper, we investigate left-invariant intrinsic chronometers (time functions) on connected finite-dimensional Lie groups. We formulate and prove sub-Lorentzian analogs of V.\,N.\,Berestovskii's classical direct and inverse theorems. A one-to-one correspondence is established between chronometers satisfying the proposed system of axioms (including upper semi-continuity and the condition that the interiors of chronological rhombi form a base for the topology) and smooth left-invariant sub-Lorentzian structures. It is shown that an axiomatic chronometer uniquely determines a closed, pointed, convex cone in the Lie algebra, whose linear span satisfies the Chow--Rashevskii condition, and an upper semi-continuous concave positively homogeneous anti-norm on it. Conversely, it is proved that any such algebraic structure satisfying a local chronologicity condition induces an intrinsic chronometer with the required properties. The proofs rely on local estimates in exponential coordinates, the Hahn--Banach separation theorem, and properties of weak limits in optimal control problems.
☆ Convergence of potential-preserving annealed Sinkhorn algorithm NeurIPS 2026
Dawid Lipinski, Maciej Buze
The annealed Sinkhorn algorithm is an iterative method for approximating solutions of optimal transport problems, in which the entropic regularisation parameter is progressively decreased. As this parameter decreases, one may preserve either the multiplicative scaling factors or the corresponding dual potentials. We study the potential-preserving iterates under positive, non-increasing regularisation schedules tending to zero. We prove that, if the schedule is non-summable, the iterates admit a subsequence converging to a solution of the corresponding optimal transport problem. The non-summability condition is sharp, as for every summable schedule in this class we construct an example in which the iterates converge to a plan violating the prescribed source marginal. We further establish convergence of the entire sequence if the relative inverse-temperature increments are also square-summable, and show by example that non-summability alone does not guarantee full convergence. Our convergence conditions are satisfied by linear inverse-temperature schedules, under which recent work has shown that the scaling-preserving iterates fail to converge to a solution of the optimal transport problem. We also derive convergence rates for polynomial inverse-temperature schedules up to and including linear growth, extending the marginal KL bound obtained by mirror-descent analysis at fixed temperature. Our best rate for the transport cost gap after rounding improves on that established for scaling-preserving annealing. Simple numerical illustrations accompany these convergence results.

☆ On convergence rate bounds for Markovian push-sum algorithms

In this work we establish an upper bound on the almost sure convergence rate of a broad class of push-sum algorithms, more precisely for those where message passing events follow a Markovian dynamics, or a Hidden Markov Model. In this context, having a computationally accessible quantity at hand is of top priority; we thus formulate tools to cut down the complexity of obtaining the stated bound. Furthermore, we introduce a transformation to adjust a given push-sum scheme in a way that the bound on the rate provably improves -- and often so does the true convergence rate. Theoretical understanding is complemented by numerical results, where the quality of all three directions is demonstrated: for the bound on the rate, for the computational complexity and for the improvement strategy.
☆ Nearly-Tight Oracle Complexity of Packing and Covering Linear Programs

We settle the deterministic oracle complexity of packing and covering linear programs, as measured by the number of oracle queries to the constraint matrix modeled by left and right matrix-vector products, up to a logarithmic factor. We do so by providing nearly-matching upper and lower bounds. Our algorithm breaks the $1/ε^2$ barrier of width-independent, $(1+ε)$-multiplicative error parallel solvers from prior work, improving the scaling with the error $ε>0$ to $1/ε,$ with total number of arithmetic operations scaling near-linearly with $1/ε$ and the number of nonzero entries of the constraint matrix.

☆ Random Feature Neural Networks for Stochastic Optimal Control
Guangyi He, Damir Filipovic, Lukas Gonon
Random feature neural networks (RFNNs) sample their hidden parameters once and train only the output layer. We analyze RFNNs as feedback policies for finite-horizon stochastic control with trajectory-dependent objectives. A policy change alters later states, so the error that matters is the objective error of the induced trajectory rather than a pointwise regression error. We extend the quantitative random-feature approximation theory for PDE solutions and nonlinear regression to feedback control. We investigate the objective error of an RFNN policy through two sources, approximation of the policy by random features and estimation of the objective from finitely many paths. A stability estimate for the controlled trajectory turns a policy error into an objective error. Under bounded actions, a regular benchmark policy and exact empirical minimization, the expected objective gap to the benchmark policy is at most of order $N^{-1/2}+\sqrt{N(1+\log N)/n}$, with $N$ the feature width per output coordinate and $n$ the number of paths. At fixed sample size the two terms trade off in $N$, and balancing them gives $N\asymp\sqrt{n/\log n}$. Across a wide range of examples, estimated gaps generally decrease with width and sample size, and RFNNs show an advantage when simulated paths are limited. We also study Parsimonious Random Feature Learning (PRFL), which grows and prunes the random dictionary during training while training only the output coefficients. At matched retained width and training budget, PRFL improves on a fixed RFNN in the LQ and Heston comparisons, while the fully trained network remains best in those examples.

Value iteration is an important tool for approximating solutions of infinite-horizon optimal control problems, but in practice it is never carried out exactly: value functions are represented by finite-dimensional approximators, and the iteration is stopped after finitely many steps. This paper analyzes which closed-loop guarantees remain under these limitations for continuous-time nonlinear systems. We consider a value iteration scheme in which each iteration solves a finite-horizon optimal control problem with the previous iterate as terminal cost, and the associated controller applies the optimal input of this problem over each horizon in a sampled-data fashion. We show that if the convergence tolerance and the approximation error are small enough, the controller asymptotically stabilizes the system on sublevel sets of the computed iterate, and provide a suboptimality bound. This condition consists of pointwise inequalities that can be checked for the computed iterate, without establishing convergence of the iteration, and is a first step towards sample-based certification. We further establish inherent robustness of the controller with respect to model errors and recover classical results for the linear-quadratic regulator. Numerical studies on a linear-quadratic problem and on a nonlinear system with known optimal value function are consistent with the guarantees and show that the suboptimality bound is conservative.

We construct a matrix analog of the Lee-Sidford barrier for semidefinite programming (SDP) with $m$ equality constraints and $n$-by-$n$ matrices. The barrier has self-concordance parameter $\widetilde{O}(m)$, so short-step interior-point methods require only $\widetilde O(\sqrt m)$ iterations. We also show that our matrix Lee-Sidford barrier can be implemented efficiently by developing a randomized algorithm that solves SDPs with $m\leq n$ to accuracy $ε$ in $(n^{ω+o(1)}+n^2m^{3/2+o(1)})\operatorname{polylog}(1/ε)$ time, where $ω\leq 9/4$ is the matrix multiplication exponent, achieving the fastest known running time in this regime.
☆ Via a New LP Relaxation: Stronger Performance Guarantees for WSEPT, and an LP-Based Proof of Kawaguchi & Kyan

Route planning during evacuations and other large-scale egress operations is inherently dynamic: the planner's recommendations affect future congestion on the roads, influence whether travelers accept their guidance, and determine what the planner can learn from the travelers' actual route choices. In this paper, we consider stochastic dynamic route recommendation to many travelers over a finite horizon under uncertain compliance and road conditions. In each period, a planner assigns routes that lead different origins' traveler groups to safe destinations, and travelers either follow the recommendation or revert to a preferred route. We model compliance using a logistic model and learn its unknown coefficients from observed route travel. We also filter the state of road conditions from noisy telemetry, and use a performance state to capture how the quality of past route recommendation affects travelers' future compliance. To determine the route assignment policy, we formulate a finite-horizon, belief-state dynamic program, show that the information state is sufficient for optimal Markov control, and develop an approximation that combines compliance beliefs with proximal policy optimization (PPO) using a Dirichlet actor over feasible route shares. We conduct numerical studies on instances of Eastern Massachusetts highway network data under different uncertain road conditions and compliance behavior. We demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of the PPO method and the value of dynamic adaptive solutions, against static routes. Our solutions reduce the mean and upper-tail costs of all travelers relative to myopic policy benchmarks, even when these benchmarks know the true compliance coefficients. Moreover, updating beliefs and the performance state dynamically also reduces the total cost under accurate, biased, and diffuse priors.

Most BO methods rely on stationary Gaussian processes, implicitly assuming that an objective black-box function exhibits homogeneous smoothness across the input space. However, many complex real-world functions have highly inhomogeneous regularity, exhibiting both smooth and rough behavior. This fundamental mismatch between the model and the black-box function severely degrades both sample efficiency and surrogate accuracy of BO. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Inhomogeneous Bayesian optimization framework. We develop a partitioned modeling strategy that dynamically subdivides the search space into subdomains, capturing spatially varying smoothness through locally adaptive kernels. To dynamically adjust the spatial resolution of the surrogate model, this approach utilizes a recursive splitting criterion. Furthermore, we develop a sampling allocation theory, establishing that driving the regional acquisition suprema below a common target level is achieved by polynomially denser sampling in rougher subdomains. Numerical experiments across homogeneous functions, synthetic inhomogeneous functions, and a real-world 8-dimensional LASSO hyperparameter tuning task demonstrate that our approach improves optimization efficiency on synthetic inhomogeneous functions, while performing comparably to Classic BO on homogeneous functions and on the LASSO task. This method favorably handles the common fixed point problem (CFPP), which requires finding a point within the intersection of finitely many constraint sets whose intersection is nonempty. Many iterative methods, including SA ones, have been proposed to solve the CFPP due to its importance in many scientific fields. We also derive semidefinite relaxation bounds and primal procedures that provide warm starts for the exact methods. The proposed approach establishes new connections between distance-based assignment, orthogonal projectors, and low-rank semidefinite optimization, and applies to general conic-representable metrics.
comment: 25 pages, 4 figures, 1 table
♻ ☆ A Dantzig-Wolfe Reformulation for Automated Aircraft Arrival Routing and Scheduling
Roghayeh Hajizadeh, Tatiana Polishchuk, Elina Rönnberg, Christiane Schmidt
We consider the problem of computing dynamic arrival routes (DARs) in a terminal maneuvering area (TMA) together with an automated scheduling of all the arrivals within a given time interval. DARs are aircraft arrival routes from all entry points of a TMA, which merge traffic in that time interval towards the runway, and are modeled as energy-efficient continuous-descent operations, such that separation based on wake-turbulence categories is guaranteed within the TMA. We propose a new model based on a Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation of a previous model for this problem. As in the previous model, we include tree consistency across consecutive planning intervals. However, the reformulation enables us to further improve the model and also consider aircraft that remain in the TMA from the previous period, a feature critical for operational safety. In computational experiments for Stockholm Arlanda airport, the new model consistently outperforms the previous one: we obtain solutions within 5 seconds to 12.65 minutes compared to up tp 40.9 hours with the old model for instances of half hours with high traffic. In addition, we are able to solve instances of a full hour of arriving aircraft with high traffic (33 aircraft) within 22.22 to 58.57 minutes, whereas the old model could not solve these instances at all. While we schedule all aircraft as continuous-descent arrivals, our model can be applied to any type of speed profiles for the arriving aircraft.
♻ ☆ Distributed Constraint-coupled Resource Allocation: Anytime Feasibility and Violation Robustness
Wenwen Wu, Shanying Zhu, Cailian Chen, Xinping Guan
This paper considers distributed resource allocation problems (DRAPs) with a coupled constraint for real-time systems. Based on primal-dual methods, we adopt a control perspective for optimization algorithm design by synthesizing a safe feedback controller using control barrier functions to enforce constraint satisfaction. On this basis, a distributed anytime-feasible resource allocation (DanyRA) algorithm is proposed. It is shown that the DanyRA algorithm converges to the exact optimal solution of DRAPs while preserving feasibility of the coupled inequality constraint from a feasible initialization. To address constraint violations caused by external disturbances, we develop a recover-after-violation mechanism using a virtual queue with a minimum buffer, enabling feasibility recovery within a prescribed number of iterations. We characterize the trade-off between convergence accuracy and violation robustness for a fixed positive buffer and establish exact convergence with a suitably decaying buffer. DanyRA is further specialized to coupled equality constraints, with constraint preservation and an explicit linear convergence rate established. Finally, a numerical example is provided for verification.
♻ ☆ Inferring behind-the-meter demand components from net load via inverse optimization
Adrian Esteban-Perez, Derek Bunn, Yashar Ghiassi-Farrokhfal
Understanding and forecasting electricity demand responses to price signals is essential to support the operational decisions of system operators, retailers, and regulators. Traditional time series and machine learning approaches have performed well under stable consumption patterns. However, the rise of active consumers with flexible assets, such as solar-plus-storage systems and electric vehicles, introduces new complexities. These consumers exhibit behind-the-meter behavior that is generally unobservable to system operators and retailers, who can typically only measure net demand at the boundary meters which are located at the connection points to the grid. Net demand reflects the aggregate of baseload consumption, flexible load shifting, and self-generation, all of which may respond nonlinearly to market prices. As these unobservable components grow, existing forecasting models may fail to capture the true dynamics of consumer behavior. This work develops and implements a data-driven inverse optimization framework to reveal behind-the-meter consumption patterns using only net demand data. By analyzing net demand as revealed at the grid connection point, we estimate parameters for a latent optimization model, enabling predictions that infer the unobservable components. This enables more accurate point and probabilistic forecasting of electricity demand under varying price signals. Thus, it provides actionable insights for system operators to improve local congestion management and flexibility extraction, as well as for retailers and aggregators, who could thereby optimize operations and tariffs to leverage consumer flexibility. We validate the methodology using real-world data, demonstrating improved forecasting accuracy over leading machine learning and time-series benchmarks.
♻ ☆ On the global convergence of gradient flow for wide shallow models beyond homogeneous nonlinearities
Romain Petit, Clarice Poon, Gabriel Peyré
A surprising phenomenon in the training of neural networks is the ability of gradient descent to find global minimizers of the training loss despite its non-convexity. Following earlier work, we investigate this behavior for wide shallow models. Existing global convergence results primarily concern models with positively one-homogeneous nonlinearities, such as ReLU activations, and models with scalar output weights and bounded nonlinearities, such as sigmoid activations. We study a broader class of models, including multi-head attention layers and two-layer fully connected networks with bounded or asymptotically positively one-homogeneous activations and vector output weights. Building upon (Chizat and Bach, 2018), we prove that, in the limit of infinitely many hidden neurons or attention heads, non-minimizers of the training loss are unstable under the mean-field gradient flow dynamics by constructing "escape regions" in the parameter space. Our global convergence statements are conditional in the following sense: if the mean-field gradient flow converges for the Wasserstein 2-distance, then its limit must be a global minimizer. We revisit the bounded nonlinearity, scalar-output setting of (Chizat and Bach, 2018), giving an escape region construction adapted to unbounded nonlinear parameter domains. We also propose new constructions for nonlinearities with at most linear growth under a non-degeneracy assumption and for asymptotically positively one-homogeneous nonlinearities. Finally, we show the well-posedness and stability estimates for the mean-field training dynamics under sub-Gaussian initializations.
♻ ☆ Linearization and local controllability of nonautonomous differential inclusions
Mira Bivas, Mihail Minkov
In this paper we study the linearization of nonautonomous differential inclusions, whose right-hand side is integrably Lipschitz in the state variable and measurable in time. We establish measurability results for time-dependent graphs and identify the Clarke tangent cone to the set of their measurable selections in $L^\infty\times L^1$. Combining this characterization with a subtransversality argument, we obtain a lower estimate for the Clarke tangent cone to the set of all admissible trajectories starting from a fixed set. As an application, we give sufficient conditions for local controllability around a closed terminal set.
♻ ★ Diffusion-Score-Based Joint Topology Identification and Generative Particle Filtering
Chuansen Peng, Xiaowei Yang, Xiaojing Shen
Inferring the interaction graph of a networked system while tracking its latent state is central to infrastructure, environmental, and brain networks. Joint identification of topology and latent states is challenging when observations are intermittent and transition noise is unknown and non-Gaussian: a flexible generative transition can absorb graph-induced changes of the conditional mean, whereas a Gaussian transition discards the information in the residual shape. We develop a diffusion-score-based framework for joint topology identification and generative particle filtering. The graph governs a leaky-diffusion conditional mean, and a frozen diffusion emulator represents the conditionally centered residual. First, a score--topology duality expresses edge-wise likelihood gradients as edge projections of the residual diffusion score, so topology learning requires neither transition densities nor differentiation through the sampler. Second, we prove identifiability from intermittent observations, invariance of the population minimizer across noise levels, and global strong convexity above an explicit smoothing threshold for bounded-plus-Gaussian residuals. With known support and oracle state pairs, the asymptotic covariance approaches the Cramér--Rao bound as smoothing vanishes and is strictly smaller than that of any Gaussian quasi-likelihood estimator under an explicit non-Gaussianity condition; for unknown sparse support we characterize the boundary limit, and we quantify the topology bias caused by residual-score mismatch. Third, we couple score-driven graph updates with an approximately fully adapted generative particle filter and prove, for bounded residuals under explicit excitation and forgetting conditions, a mean-square closed-loop bound with a step-size-independent small-gain condition. Synthetic and real-data experiments confirm these gains under non-Gaussian forcing.
♻ ☆ The Loss Does Not See the Basis, but Adam Does
Devender Singh
Different optimization algorithms can find very different solutions to the same problem. Gradient descent (GD) exhibits a low-rank bias in overparameterized problems when initialized near zero, while Adam does not. GD is rotationally equivariant: rotating both factors of a factored model $W = UV^\top$ by an orthogonal matrix leaves the loss unchanged, and GD's solution rotates accordingly. In contrast, Adam is not. We show that any algorithm using only the current gradient and respecting rotational symmetry amounts to a left-preconditioner depending only on the gradient's Gram matrix. This gives a norm-based test, which passes for the spectral norm in Muon and fails for Adam's $\ell_\infty$ norm. Empirically, nine optimizers fall into groups consistent with the test on underdetermined matrix sensing. Sharing Adam's second moment across coordinates gradually recovers a low-rank bias, and its solutions approach GD's as the stepsize decreases. On four hyperspectral scenes, Adam's solutions are hundreds to thousands of times further from GD's than two GD runs with different step sizes are from each other. In transformers and LoRA adapters, Adam separates two rotationally equivalent models from the first iteration, and learns higher-rank attention updates. Overall, recovering particular solutions depends on the optimizer's invisible coordinate basis, as well as how fast it grows small singular values relative to large ones.

♻ ☆ Characterization of stability radii for robustly asymptotically stable dissipative Hamiltonian differential-algebraic systems
Peter Benner, Volker Mehrmann, Anshul Prajapati, Punit Sharma
We study linear time-invariant dissipative Hamiltonian differential-algebraic systems. We characterize when the systems are robustly asymptotically stable and derive exact conditions and bounds when this property is lost under structure-preserving perturbations.
♻ ☆ Rare Event Analysis via Stochastic Optimal Control
Yuanqi Du, Jiajun He, Dinghuai Zhang, Eric Vanden-Eijnden, Carles Domingo-Enrich
Rare events, from biomolecular conformational changes and phase transitions to chemical reactions, are central to many physical systems, yet extremely difficult to study computationally because unbiased simulations seldom produce them. Transition Path Theory provides a rigorous statistical framework for analyzing such events: it characterizes the ensemble of reactive trajectories between two metastable states (reactant and product), and its central object, the committor function (the probability that the system next reaches the product rather than the reactant), encodes essential kinetic and thermodynamic information. We introduce a framework for committor estimation that builds on stochastic optimal control, with a principled formulation that grounds committor learning on capped hitting-time trajectories. In this framework the committor defines a feedback control, proportional to the gradient of its logarithm, that steers trajectories toward the reactive region, enabling sampling of reactive paths. As practical algorithms, we develop two training losses: a heuristic on-policy direct backpropagation loss and a principled off-policy Value Matching loss, for which we establish first-order optimality guarantees. Being off-policy, Value Matching can leverage simulated trajectories from alternative sampling processes and reuse them from a replay buffer, which enables efficient learning. In particular, we derive a reactive current-preserving sampling process that can accelerate exploration. On reversible and non-reversible dynamics, the framework yields more accurate committor estimates, reaction rates, and transition path samples than existing methods.
♻ ☆ One-sided certification of surrogate near-minimizers: exact worst-case envelopes under strong convexity and smoothness
Karim Bounja, Boujemaâ Achchab, Abdeljalil Sakat
We study target suboptimality for points that approximately minimize a surrogate objective. Unlike standard uniform perturbation estimates, the available comparison is one-sided, thresholded at a certified lower target level, and restricted to the entire surrogate-selected sublevel set. We first show that selected comparison alone cannot yield a finite worst-case guarantee, even for strongly convex quadratics with identical Hessians. A single scalar upper bound on the surrogate minimum closes this information gap and leads to a sharp general estimate. For pairs of $μ$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth objectives, we then solve the associated worst-case information problem exactly. We obtain a sharp feasibility barrier and a dimension-free envelope; in its nontrivial regime, the value reduces to a scalar maximization over a compact interval. Explicit one-dimensional piecewise-quadratic objectives attain the bound while satisfying the one-sided constraint on the full selected set. We characterize when curvature strictly improves the general certificate and provide a threshold-preserving finite-net validation procedure. The results identify the best guarantee permitted by the prescribed partial information, independently of any particular optimization algorithm or additive perturbation model.

♻ ☆ A Trust-Region Interior-Point Stochastic Sequential Quadratic Programming Method
Yuchen Fang, Jihun Kim, Sen Na, James Demmel, Javad Lavaei
In this paper, we propose a trust-region interior-point stochastic sequential quadratic programming (TR-IP-SSQP) method for solving optimization problems with a stochastic objective and deterministic nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. In this setting, exact evaluations of the objective function and its gradient are unavailable, but their stochastic estimates can be constructed. In particular, at each iteration our method builds stochastic oracles whose estimates of the objective value and gradient satisfy proper adaptive accuracy conditions with a fixed probability. To handle inequality constraints, we adopt an interior-point method (IPM), in which the barrier parameter is taken from a prescribed decreasing sequence and is reduced once a stochastic stationarity test is passed. Under standard assumptions, we show that, almost surely, the KKT residual vanishes along the iterations at which the barrier parameter is reduced, and every limit point of these iterates is a KKT point. We implement the method on a subset of problems from the CUTEst test set, as well as on constrained logistic regression problems, to demonstrate its practical performance.
♻ ☆ Ellipsoid Separation in Data-Dependent Time via Infimal Displacement Vectors
Matthew Hough, Stephen A. Vavasis
The infimal displacement vector of the nonexpansive operator underlying the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm (PDHG) is known to encode useful information for infeasible optimization problems. In particular, for the ellipsoid separation problem (ESP), where the goal is to find a separating hyperplane between two collections of ellipsoids, the infimal displacement vector corresponding to an infeasible second-order cone program (SOCP) encodes a separating hyperplane. We show FISTA computes a sequence of approximations to the dual component of the infimal displacement vector and establish that a solution to the ESP can be obtained in $\mathcal{O}(δ_{\mathcal{A}}^{-2})$ iterations. We then show how to improve the bound to $\mathcal{O}(δ_{\mathcal{A}}^{-1})$. Here $δ_{\mathcal{A}}$ denotes the distance between the convex hulls of the two ellipsoid collections.
♻ ☆ On the Impact of Alternative Settlement Rules for State-of-Charge-Limited Resources in Electricity Markets
Alexandre Moreira
Standard two-settlement markets compute a participant's total profit as the sum of its day-ahead (DA) profit and its incremental real-time (RT) profit. This rule was designed for conventional generators, which can always deliver their DA schedules in RT because their capacity is the same in both markets. Energy storage resources, in contrast, are limited by their state of charge (SOC), so their ability to honor a DA award depends on the SOC available at the time of RT dispatch. When this SOC is insufficient, the RT market may impose a buy-back or sell-back that can lead to a monetary loss. This paper formalizes this asymmetry between SOC-unlimited and SOC-limited resources and assesses three alternative settlement rules: a zero-profit floor; a max rule, which pays storage the maximum of its RT-only profit and its standard DA plus incremental RT profit; and a variant of the max rule applied only when the standard profit is negative. Through our analysis and a case study based on a realistic version of the California system, we identify when storage is most exposed to losses, assess how the alternative rules let storage deviate from DA awards to provide flexibility, and quantify their impact on revenue adequacy.
♻ ☆ Tube-Based Robust Data-Driven Predictive Control for Linear Time-Invariant Systems
Chi Wang, David Angeli
This paper presents a tractable tube-based robust data-driven predictive control scheme that uses only a single finite noisy input-state trajectory of an unknown discrete-time linear time-invariant (LTI) system. A simplex constraint is imposed on the Hankel coefficient vector, yielding explicit polyhedral bounds on the prediction mismatch induced by bounded measurement noise. Using certified initial and terminal robust positively invariant (RPI) sets, we derive a tube-tightened formulation whose online optimization problem is a strictly convex quadratic program (QP). The resulting controller guarantees recursive feasibility, robust satisfaction of input and state constraints, and practical input-to-state stability of the closed loop with respect to measurement noise. Numerical examples illustrate the effectiveness, robustness, and closed-loop performance of the proposed method.
♻ ☆ Quadrature-Induced Local Minima in Structure-Preserving Lotka-Volterra Control
Alexandre Autran
We study how the choice of harvest quadrature affects optimal control in a positivity-preserving Lotka--Volterra scheme. With harvesting alone, counting the prey removed at each step gives a strictly convex cost. Using the prey density at the start of the step overestimates the catch and can create a strict local minimum with cost above the global minimum. We certify the global minimizers in a two-step example by rational root isolation. A second example shows that, with both species present and positive diffusion, a strict local minimizer for the old-state rule admits a descent direction under the flux rule. For nonnegative $H^1$ initial data and positive diffusivities in one space dimension, the two rules give costs, weighted gradients and Hessians that differ by $O(τ)$ at the same control, uniformly in the spatial mesh. Here $τ$ is the time step. If the old-state Hessian is uniformly coercive near a stationary control, the flux objective has a local minimizer within $O(τ)$ of it. With uniformly bounded tracking targets, a large enough effort penalty makes both objectives strongly convex for all sufficiently small time steps. We also derive exact discrete adjoints and Hessian actions, prove a common variational limit with an IMEX discretization, and compare stationary controls across grids. The same harvest accounting applies to weighted production--destruction systems.

♻ ☆ Randomized Forward Mode of Automatic Differentiation For Optimization Algorithms
Khemraj Shukla, Yeonjong Shin
Reverse mode automatic differentiation (AD) computes a gradient in a single sweep, but at a memory cost that grows with the length of the computational graph. That cost becomes the binding constraint when the graph is long, as in parameter identification governed by differential equations or in training on memory-limited hardware. We study a randomized forward mode gradient (RFG) as an alternative to backpropagation in precisely this regime. RFG is a random gradient estimator built from the directional derivative along a random vector, a quantity that forward mode AD computes without storing a tape. Replacing the gradient with RFG yields a class of optimization algorithms; for RFG-based gradient descent (GD) and Polyak's heavy ball (PHB) methods, we establish convergence results on quadratic functions. The analysis reveals that using random vectors from a probability distribution with the smallest kurtosis yields the fastest rate of convergence. Computational experiments demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithms and verify the theoretical findings, including beyond quadratic functions. We further characterize when RFG is computationally preferable to backpropagation. Since the variance of RFG grows with the parameter dimension $d$ while the memory required by the reverse mode grows with the length $\ell$ of the computational graph, the relevant figure of merit is the ratio $\ell/d$. We confirm this by measurement against reverse mode with checkpointing. For a physics-informed neural network, where $d$ is large and $\ell$ short, RFG is not competitive. For parameter identification governed by differential equations, where a handful of coefficients is recovered from a long time integration, RFG requires one to three orders of magnitude less memory. The price is a larger iteration count, which leaves its time to solution comparable to or worse than a well-tuned reverse mode.
comment: 38 Pages, 9 Figures
♻ ☆ Minimal Control Time of Large Generic Quantum Systems at Critical Spectral Growth
Thomas Chambrion, Cristian Mendico
The minimal time needed to steer a closed quantum system between two arbitrary states is a fundamental performance limit of quantum control. For single-input bilinear Schrödinger systems of dimension $d$ with unbounded controls, this state-to-state control time is bounded from above by the weight $M_d$ of a minimum spanning tree (MST) built from the drift Hamiltonian written in the eigenbasis of the control Hamiltonian. We ask whether the control time of a \emph{generic} system, whose control Hamiltonian has a Haar-distributed eigenbasis, vanishes as $d\to\infty$ in the critical regime of drift eigenvalues growing as $k^{3/2}$. We prove that the finite clusters of the interaction matrix are asymptotically independent Gaussians, analyse the resulting independent surrogate model, for which $M_d \asymp (\ln d)^{-1/2}$ with an explicit finite-size expansion predicting $M_d\sqrt{\ln d}\to 10/3$, and test the exact Haar model by Monte Carlo simulations up to $d=18101$. The exact and surrogate models are statistically indistinguishable in mean at all tested dimensions, and both are consistent with the predicted limit, supporting the conjecture that the control time vanishes, albeit only logarithmically.

♻ ☆ Extended Set-based Tasks for Multi-task Execution and Prioritization
Gennaro Notomista, Mario Selvaggio, Francesca Pagano, María Santos, Siddharth Mayya, Vincenzo Lippiello, Cristian Secchi
The ability of executing multiple tasks simultaneously is an important feature of redundant robotic systems. As a matter of fact, complex behaviors can often be obtained as a result of the execution of several tasks. Moreover, in safety-critical applications, tasks designed to ensure the safety of the robot and its surroundings have to be executed along with other nominal tasks. In such cases, it is also important to prioritize the former over the latter. In this paper, we formalize the definition of extended set-based tasks, i.e., tasks which can be executed by rendering subsets of the task space asymptotically stable or forward invariant using control barrier functions. We propose a formal mathematical representation of such tasks that allows for the execution of more complex and time-varying prioritized stacks of tasks using kinematic and dynamic robot models alike. We present an optimization-based framework which is computationally efficient, accounts for input bounds, and allows for the stable execution of time-varying prioritized stacks of extended set-based tasks. The proposed framework is validated using extensive simulations, quantitative comparisons to the state-of-the-art hierarchical quadratic programming, and experiments with robotic manipulators.
♻ ☆ Using delays for prescribed-time static output feedback stabilization of LTI controllable and observable systems
Kang-Kang Zhang, Emilia Fridman
This paper addresses a stabilization problem: can every controllable and observable LTI system be stabilized by static output feedback (SOF)? To the best of our knowledge, we provide, for the first time, a solution to this problem. Furthermore, the proposed design achieves prescribed-time convergence to the origin independently of the initial condition. Two SOF methods are developed. The first employs multiple artificial discrete output delays with smooth time-varying gains and provides an explicit gain construction for every controllable and observable LTI system, based on a generalized controllability--observability Gramian introduced in this paper. The second combines constant-gain feedback of the current output with time-varying-gain feedback of a single artificially delayed output and also applies to every controllable and observable LTI system. Its simpler structure requires auxiliary parameters whose existence is guaranteed but whose explicit construction is provided only for SISO systems. The multiple-delay design is further extended to known bounded and fast-varying (without any constraints on the delay derivative) measurement delays that may be large, yielding fixed-time stabilization under a corresponding rank condition, with an assignable settling-time bound greater than three times the delay bound. For practical implementation, we further present an SOF controller with time-varying gains that depends on discrete-time delayed measurements. For unknown constant measurement or input delays, fixed-time stabilization is established for systems with nilpotent state matrices. A numerical implementation of Gramian-based gains is also suggested. Numerical examples involving nonminimum-phase, flexible-structure, and cart--pole systems illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

☆ Dynamics Forcing: Mitigating Error Accumulation in Causal Video World Models
Xin Zhou, Cong Miao
Causal video world models generate block by block from their own previous outputs. Small errors in early blocks are fed back as history and grow until the scene and the robot fall apart. Teacher forcing trains on clean ground-truth history, so the model never sees the history it will actually condition on, and it also finds a shortcut: copying the previous frame instead of predicting how the scene changes. We present Dynamics Forcing, a training scheme that keeps real video as the only supervision and reshapes how history is presented. History is perturbed in three ways: random noising, self-resampling by the model itself, and joint denoising, in which the most recent blocks are still partly noisy when the next block is predicted. On top of this we move history guidance and first-frame anchor guidance from inference into training, so that the model is pushed to use its history and its reference frame rather than ignore them. Dynamics Forcing needs no teacher model, no distillation, and no additional model at inference. Applied to a 5B video model with LoRA on 77 hours of manipulation video on a single GPU, it better matches unseen real continuations and reduces error accumulation.
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables
☆ How Should a Home Robot Update Its Memories When Human Routines Change? CoRL 2026
Oliver Wang, Mani Srivastava
A home robot that helps with chores needs to know where objects are, but people move objects according to routines that change and later change back. The robot's memory must adapt to the new routine without erasing experience that may become useful again. One approach is to have a language model maintain written summaries of the home from the robot's own observations, but existing evaluations of such memories use static worlds. We explore simulated households where a resident gets sick, recovers, and later gets sick again. We compare a rule that keeps every room an object has been seen in, language-model memories that store only written summaries, and language-model memories that can also read the raw history of sightings. The rule outperforms every summary-only memory, and giving language models the sighting history closes the gap. Surprisingly, writing summaries on top of the history adds nothing we can measure. When the illness returns, methods that keep the history search better than they did the first time, while summary-only methods show no consistent improvement. Deleting the first illness from memory removes all of the rule's gain and part of theirs. The summaries recorded where objects went during the illness but rarely distinguished sick-day patterns from normal routines. Our findings suggest that common approaches to summarizing robot memories struggle to remember facts about a routine that might return, highlighting the need for future benchmarks to evaluate this aspect of long-term robot deployment.

☆ Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head for Tiny Vision-Language-Action Models
Aditya Makineni, Amitesh Sahoo, Qing Tian
Real-time onboard robot control calls for a lightweight vision-language-action (VLA) model, yet shrinking the backbone leaves less capacity for deliberation at inference time. Chain-of-thought decoding, dual-system architectures, and larger backbones can restore deliberation but reintroduce the latency and memory costs that motivated going small. Recurrent action heads offer a lighter alternative by iterating in latent space before committing to an action, but existing designs refine a single undifferentiated state that must simultaneously encode slowly evolving task context and rapidly changing motor commands. We propose the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH), which maintains two latent states updated at different frequencies: a low-level state that updates fast, grounded in action tokens and proprioception, and a high-level state that updates slowly, grounded in visual understanding and the instruction-informed low-level state. The two states exchange information through nested reasoning cycles. Because all iteration occurs in the compact head after a single backbone pass, HR-AH adds hierarchical reasoning without increasing the backbone size. With a 22.5M-parameter head, 3-4.3x smaller than those of RD-VLA and VLA-Adapter on the same backbone, HR-AH reaches 97.0% success rate on LIBERO and a 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC->D, at the lowest latency among compared methods. We show that this hierarchy improves performance over a parameter-matched single-state head, and that routing distinct modalities to each level yields further gains in both accuracy and inference cost.

☆ Superellipse Function: A Powerful Geometric Tool for the Design and Deformation Modeling of Tendon-Driven Continuum Manipulators With Flexural Patterns Experiencing Tension Loss
Yang Liu, Farshid Alambeigi
In this article, we feature the Superellipse function as a geometric and versatile tool for effective design and modeling of flexural patterns (FPs) in tendon-driven continuum manipulators (TD-CMs) with discontinuous cross section geometries. We also propose a unique complementary mathematical framework and solution algorithm for modeling the effects of distributed and concentrated friction forces- caused by partially-constrained tendons- on tension loss and deformation behavior of a TD-CM designed using a Superellipse function. Particularly, by employing this geometric function, we establish four intuitive functional mappings relating the manipulator's geometric parameters, kinematics, and deformation behavior. Thanks to the features of these intuitive mappings and Superellipse function, we then introduce the concepts of design space and design curve to facilitate intuitive design of a TD-CM with a generic FP geometry experiencing tendon tension loss. To thoroughly evaluate the performance of this novel framework and its aforementioned features, we performed various simulation and experimental studies on TD-CMs designed and fabricated based on a Superellipse function. Results were then analyzed and compared using different error metrics.
☆ Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios from Role-Typed Signal Temporal Logic Specifications Drafted by Large Language Models
Zifan Zeng, Qunli Zhang, Peng Wang, Shiming Liu, Feng Liu, Zheng Hu
Safety-critical scenarios are rare in recorded driving and must be generated to test and train motion planners of automated vehicles. In guided diffusion models, each scenario type needs its own weighted objective, separate from the validity check. Optimized together with the attacker, the vehicle under test can cancel the attack or draw it toward itself. We state each scenario as a signal temporal logic specification with clauses typed by role. Every clause names the agent it may change and the agents it may read, and the vehicle under test reads the attacker only from the attack onset. A large language model drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker accepts it. A compiler derives the optimization: it edits a diffusion model's samples by the smallest change that satisfies the specification, each clause moves only its owner, the attacker is solved against the unreacted vehicle under test before its response, and the monitor of the same specification decides acceptance. On nuScenes and CommonRoad, judged independently of the specification, one parameter set produced valid scenarios at a rate 0.14 above a weighted objective tuned per scenario type, and descriptions yielded at least one valid scenario for 11 of the 16 pre-crash types expressible in the public data. Learned planners fail more often on the generated scenarios than on their seeds. Fine-tuning on them lowers a planner's failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.

☆ Into My Arms: Structured reinforcement learning for autonomous transport of objects and humans
Elle Miller, Reem Almheiri, Takuma Tsukakoshi, Ben Sanati, Tamon Miyake, Yushi Wang, Namiko Saito, Shigeki Sugano, Tetsuya Ogata, Rika Antonova, Oisin Mac Aodha, Sethu Vijayakumar
Whole-body humanoid manipulation remains bottlenecked by high-dimensional state-action spaces, contact-rich environments, and long task horizons. This trilemma is a challenge that state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) methods are yet to resolve reliably. We address it with three contributions that add just enough structure to guide exploration: Sparse Interaction Edges (SIE) for whole-body manipulation, Interaction Gated Transport (IGT) for sustained transport over long horizons, and a Hinted Object Path (HOP) that resolves collision and search complexity bottlenecks. Across all three, the policy remains free to discover its own manipulation strategy. The method generalises from rigid object to human transport. As a flagship demonstration, we show, to our knowledge, the first bed-to-wheelchair transfer of a medical mannequin by a humanoid robot completed with no human intervention during execution. In the domain of human transfer, we show that a single policy can adapt across substantial variations in body mass, size, and random force perturbations, all while training on a single GPU in under an hour. Our approach offers a pathway to fully RL-driven humanoid manipulation, enabling assistive robots that can help humans. Website: https://elle-miller.github.io/into_my_arms
